articles.title: 'Breaking Bad' to 'Prison Break': Stalin takes fresh swipe at Vijay govt after 17 inmates flee jail
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu CM MK Stalin on Tuesday launched a fresh cinematic salvo at the ruling TVK government, following up his 'Breaking Bad' jibe
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Tamil Nadu CM MK Stalin on Tuesday launched a fresh cinematic salvo at the ruling TVK government, following up his 'Breaking Bad' jibe with a 'Prison Break' reference to target chief minister C Joseph Vijay over the escape of 17 inmates from a Theni sub-jail.The DMK supremo's remarks came after 17 undertrial inmates allegedly escaped from Thekkampatti sub-jail in Tamil Nadu's Theni district late on Monday night.Former CM hit out at the TVK government, accusing the administration of failing to maintain law and order.Taking a swipe at the government led by actor-turned-politician Vijay, Stalin drew a parallel with the television series Prison Break, saying the state appeared to be witnessing a similar situation after two prisoners had earlier escaped from Puzhal prison.“Following Breaking Bad, Prison Break has now begun in Tamil Nadu too!” Stalin said in a post on X, questioning how such a large number of inmates could escape despite improved security arrangements and surveillance systems.He said the escape of 17 inmates was particularly alarming, mentioning that it was reportedly the first such incident since 1995. Stalin said the incident came soon after the escape of two prisoners from Puzhal prison, raising questions over prison security.Accusing the government of incompetence, the former chief minister said authorities had failed to keep track of criminals released on bail and were now struggling to prevent escapes from inside jails.“Criminals outside are committing crimes freely. Prisoners inside are also escaping without fear,” he said.Stalin further alleged that the TVK government was incapable of protecting the people of Tamil Nadu, describing it as a “completely useless, good-for-nothing administration”.He said the state had reached a point where people were being left to fend for themselves, and demanded accountability over the security lapses.This is not the first time Stalin has used a cinematic reference to target Vijay's government. Days earlier, he invoked 'Breaking Bad' following a multi-crore methamphetamine seizure in the state.The political attack followed the arrest of Boopalan, a TVK Nagapattinam district functionary and the party's Kilvelur election in-charge, by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence (DRI). He was arrested for allegedly harbouring 135kg of methamphetamine, reportedly worth several crores of rupees.How 17 inmates allegedly escapedAccording to preliminary investigations, the 17 undertrial inmates allegedly feigned epileptic seizures to lure prison staff into opening their cell before attacking the guards and fleeing the premises.The incident took place at Thekkampatti sub-jail in Theni district late on Monday night. Four of the escapees have been rearrested, while 13 remain at large.Three prison personnel were injured in the incident. Grade II Police Constable Thangapandi suffered serious head injuries and was rushed to the Government Hospital at G Vilakku. Two other personnel sustained minor injuries.Praveen Kumar was the first of the four escapees to be caught. The other three, identified as Silambarasan of Theni and Raja Sikandar and Rajkumar of Madurai, were re-arrested during search operations on Tuesday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: A three-year-old boy named Nevada Pierre has gone viral after a dispute at a youth soccer game in Winter Park, Florida, led a league official to call the
articles.body: A three-year-old boy named Nevada Pierre has gone viral after a dispute at a youth soccer game in Winter Park, Florida, led a league official to call the police. Videos shared by his family show the toddler dribbling past older opponents and scoring goals, prompting his parents to allege that he was being excluded because he was too good at the game. The league official, however, told officers that Nevada had allegedly pushed other players and that his parents had argued with him over playing-time decisions. articles.summary: Land Rover has reduced prices of the Defender 110 in India following the start of local assembly, with prices dropping by up to Rs 34 lakh compared to the
articles.body: Land Rover has reduced prices of the Defender 110 in India following the start of local assembly, with prices dropping by up to Rs 34 lakh compared to the earlier completely built-up (CBU) import models. The SUV is now assembled in India through the completely knocked down (CKD) route, with the X-Dynamic HSE trim available with three engine options.The Defender 110 3.0-litre diesel D350 and 3.0-litre petrol P400 variants are now priced at Rs 1.18 crore each, down from Rs 1.52 crore previously. This translates to a price reduction of Rs 34 lakh for both versions. The entry-level 2.0-litre petrol P300 variant is now priced at Rs 99 lakh, compared to its earlier CBU price of Rs 1.135 crore, making it Rs 14.5 lakh cheaper. India is the second country globally to manufacture the Defender, after Slovakia.The local assembly programme also brings additional equipment to the Defender 110, with several features that were previously available as paid optional extras now included as standard. The D350 diesel and P400 petrol variants gain 29 such features, while the P300 petrol version gets 17 additional features as standard. These options were reportedly popular among buyers, with most customers opting for them on the CBU models.Common additions across the lineup include electronic air suspension, Adaptive Dynamics, Terrain Response 2, Adaptive Off-Road Cruise Control, a solar-attenuating windscreen, headlight power wash and a body-coloured spare wheel cover. The P300 petrol variant also gets a ClearSight interior rear-view mirror, a front centre console refrigerator compartment and three-zone climate control with rear cooling assist.The D350 and P400 versions receive additional equipment, including Configurable Terrain Response, an electronic active differential with torque vectoring by braking, 20-inch diamond-turned alloy wheels, heated third-row seats and 14-way electrically adjustable front seats with heating, cooling and memory functions.The two higher-specification engine options also benefit from interior upgrades, including Windsor leather and Kvadrat seats, a suedecloth headlining, a Meridian surround sound system and a head-up display. Other additions include Cabin Air Purification Plus, an air quality sensor, a ClearSight interior rear-view mirror, a refrigerated front centre console compartment and three-zone climate control with rear cooling assist.Land Rover Defender 110: Engine and performanceThe locally assembled Defender 110 continues with three powertrain options, all paired with an eight-speed automatic transmission. The D350 diesel uses a 3.0-litre engine producing 350 PS and 700 Nm of torque. The P400 petrol gets a 3.0-litre engine generating 400 PS and 550 Nm, while the P300 is powered by a 2.0-litre petrol engine producing 300 PS and 400 Nm.In terms of acceleration, the D350 can sprint from 0 to 100 kmph in 6.4 seconds. The P400 completes the same run in 6.1 seconds, while the P300 takes 7.4 seconds.The Defender 110's off-road capability is supported by its electronic air suspension, which can raise the vehicle by up to 75 mm in off-road height mode, taking ground clearance to 293 mm. The suspension can also lower the SUV by up to 50 mm in access height mode.Other equipment includes Matrix LED headlights, all-terrain tyres, a full-size spare wheel, a sliding panoramic roof and wireless device charging. The SUV also features the Pivi Pro infotainment system with a 13.1-inch curved HD touchscreen.For water crossings, the Defender gets Wade Sensing, which displays water depth and alerts the driver as the vehicle approaches its maximum wading depth of 900 mm.

articles.title: SC seeks Centre’s response to media body’s plea challenging data protection act
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Centre on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) challenging
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Tuesday issued notice to the Centre on a petition filed by the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) challenging provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act and its accompanying rules. The association had alleged that the act infringe press freedom and the right to information.A bench comprising Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the notice after hearing senior advocate Madhavi Divan, appearing for the DNPA. The matter will be heard next on November 17 along with pending petitions.The plea seeks to strike down several provisions of the law, arguing that the absence of an exemption for journalistic activities could impede reporting, undermine investigative journalism and compromise the confidentiality of sources.Describing the petition as a comprehensive challenge by traditional news organisations, Divan told the bench, “This is perhaps the first comprehensive petition by what we call legacy media. There has been some debate over citizen journalists. We are the traditional, conventional legacy media.”She sought an interim stay on the challenged provisions, arguing that consent requirements could make routine and time-sensitive reporting difficult.“If I am left to the mercy of the data principal as to whether he or she will give consent, how will news be reported?” she asked.Divan also warned that the provisions could affect live television coverage and restrict newsrooms from reporting without prior permission.“What is the point if I have to ask for permission and consent,” she asked.According to Reuters, media groups told the court that the law amounted to pre-censorship and could force newsrooms to shut down. The challenge involves 21 news publishers.RTI amendment also challengedThe DNPA has also challenged the amendment to Section 8(1)(j) of the Right to Information (RTI) Act, arguing that it restricts access to information and limits public scrutiny.“Section 8(1)(j), the deletion, is changing the whole concept of news,” Divan submitted according to news agency PTI.The petition further questions the Centre’s powers to requisition information under the DPDP Act, claiming they could affect news organisations’ ability to report on matters of public interest.The Supreme Court is scheduled to hear the matter on November 17 alongside pending cases.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: MPs and MSP detained by Israel and barred from entering West Bank
articles.summary: SNP MP Lara Bird and the Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens were part of an international delegation turned away by Israeli security forces.
articles.body:
Two MPs and an MSP have said they were detained by Israeli authorities for eight hours while trying to enter the West Bank.

SNP MP Lara Bird, Labour MP Clive Lewis and Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens said they were prevented from entering the territory on Monday before being questioned and eventually turned away.

Bird said in a social media post that they had intended to "stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land".

They had travelled to the region as part of a Progressive International delegation that also included ex-Labour MP Sam Tarry and a former member of the Basque senate.

The Israeli military announced on Monday that all West Bank land crossings would be closed as part of increased security measures during Tuesday's national elections .

Posting on Instagram, Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, said the 23-strong group was "interrogated and ultimately prevented from crossing" the King Hussein Bridge between Jordan and the West Bank.

Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy

Lewis, who represents Norwich South, said the group had been "made to feel as though they had done something wrong" in a post on X.

He added: "We knew that by crossing into the occupied Palestinian territories, we risked being detained, interrogated and turned away by Israeli authorities. And that, alas, is exactly what happened.

"The simple truth is we had done nothing wrong. We went to show our support for the Palestinian people and highlight the terrible injustice and violence being perpetrated against them."

Nevens described the experience as "frightening" but added that the group was able to "leave safely".

She said: "What we experienced was only a small fraction of the terrifying reality Palestinians face when they try to cross the same border to reach their families or simply go about their lives."

About 2,000 Palestinian residents have been displaced in Hebron, a city in the southern West Bank, in recent days.

Footage shared online appeared to show one street being completely flattened by bulldozers .

That came as a reprisal for the killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinian gunmen.

Several other attacks on Palestinians during the annual olive harvest have also been reported in the run-up to the elections.

They are the first since the 7 October Hamas-led attack on Israel in 2023.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the Commons the UK government was "deeply concerned" about MPs and MSP being denied access to the West Bank.

He said the government had raised the issue with the Israeli authorities and had been in touch with the MPs to offer assistance.

"More broadly, it's very, very important that members of this House, as they go about their business – not just in the UK but internationally – have free access so that they can actually do their duties," he said.

A spokesperson for the SNP said the party was "proud to stand with the Palestinian people".

The Israeli embassy has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Flood-weary U.S. Southwest eyes forecast for more rain
articles.summary: More flooding made parts of the normally arid Four Corners region look more like an ocean than a desert, as locals kept a wary eye on a forecast for still more rain ahead.
articles.body: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M — More flooding made parts of the normally arid Four Corners region look more like an ocean than a desert Monday, as locals kept a wary eye on a forecast for still more rain ahead. Damage in New Mexico alone after more than four days of flooding — only the latest in a deadly autumn of soaking rains in the U.S. Southwest — could total $300 million, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham said. The latest town to evacuate was tiny Bluff in southeastern Utah after San Juan River flooding swamped parts of cities and towns upstream in Colorado and New Mexico. With parts of his town of 250 underwater, Mayor Josh Ewing was worried by a forecast for yet more heavy rain this weekend. After a few days of sunny, dry weather, more rounds of rain are predicted Friday night and again on Sunday, according to the National Weather Service. “It’s the second flood that really gets you, you know, because everything is completely saturated. And so we’re trying to recover fast enough to be on alert for what might happen,” Ewing said. New Mexico assesses damage, awaits aid Upstream from Bluff, in Farmington, New Mexico, Pagosa Springs, Colorado, and elsewhere along the San Juan and Animas rivers, hundreds of homes remained evacuated or cut off by flooded roads. Many homes were still without power as officials assessed when it would be safe for residents to return and have their utilities turned back on. President Donald Trump on Monday announced federal disaster assistance would be available to New Mexico with 25% to be matched by agencies in the state. Earlier in the day, Lujan Grisham expressed concern about the matching requirement but said she would “frontload” state resources for flood recovery. She estimated that the costs of debris removal, road and bridge repair and other “longhaul” recovery could amount to as much as $300 million. “I don’t care if it’s a billion dollars. The goal here is to identify every state, every federal, every local resource and get it where it belongs,” Lujan Grisham said. At least two deaths were reported in New Mexico. Isabelle Beulaygue, 39, was swept away while attempting to cross a flooded arroyo in a vehicle Saturday in Santa Fe, authorities said. About 50 miles (80 kilometers) south in Socorro County, 64-year-old Grace Clark was swept away as floodwaters rose and trapped residents in their homes. Valencia County Fire Chief Matthew Propp said nine other people were rescued as teams worked overnight to find residents. Between 200 and 300 people in San Juan County, New Mexico, were rescued in the last few days, according to county spokesperson Devin Neeley. Damage spread onto the vast Navajo Nation spanning parts of Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. Lupita Villa, her husband and three young children evacuated their rental home along the San Juan River in Farmington on Thursday. When they returned on Saturday, they needed muck boots and waders to reach the front door. Once inside, they found their laminate floors warped under several inches of muddy floodwater and much of their furniture destroyed. The family is staying with relatives on higher ground while they plan next steps. Villa said her children are struggling to understand that their former home is now unlivable. “They just keep asking, ‘When can we go back?’” Villa said. Colorado residents still cut off by washed-out roads The crisis continued in southern Colorado’s Archuleta County. After more rain brought another surge in San Juan River flooding through the hot springs resort town of Pagosa Springs last weekend, the river was back below flood stage Monday for the first time in more than three days. No further rescues were reported after air operations that included the rescue of two people, three dogs and two cats from a recreational vehicle washed downstream in floodwaters Friday. But all evacuated areas remained closed. Responders were landing in helicopters to check on people still unable to leave their homes due to the floodwaters and road damage. “We do have a number of people cut off still but we’re accessing those with the National Guard and our search and rescue crews,” Archuleta County Sheriff Mike Le Roux said. Utah town surveys desert that now looks like a sea Officials throughout the region cautioned people to avoid entering floodwaters after wastewater treatment plants got flooded. If you are exposed, they said, take a shower or bath as soon as possible. In Montezuma Creek, 14 miles (22 kilometers) downstream from Bluff, the Navajo Tribal Utility Authority reported its wastewater treatment lagoons were “completely breached,” potentially contaminating the San Juan River with bacteria and pathogens. The river crested Monday lower than expected in Bluff. The water stopped mostly short of a highway that runs through town, said Ewing, the mayor and a local firefighter who took part in flood rescues. It was cold comfort, though, after floodwaters hit seven more homes and four businesses overnight to bring the local flood toll to 17 homes and five businesses since a surge on Friday. Unlike flooding that followed a levee break Friday, Ewing said, the latest surge happened after a day of warnings that higher water was on the way. “It’s kind a weird thing when you’ve lived in red rock country to feel like you live by the sea now. Our flood plain is just filled,” Ewing said.

articles.title: Early Israeli election turnout highest in decades as Netanyahu fights to keep power
articles.summary: The first vote since the October 7 attacks is a tight race between Benjamin Netanyahu and ex-military chief Gadi Eisenkot — with the future direction of Israel at stake. Follow for live updates.
articles.body:
• Crucial election : Turnout in the first few hours of voting in Israel’s election remains at the highest levels in more than 50 years. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has cast his ballot in an important election seen as a referendum on his leadership since the October 7, 2023 attacks.

• Key timings: Polls will close at 10 p.m. local time (4 p.m. ET). Opinion polls suggest the race will be too close to call, with Netanyahu in a tight race against Gadi Eisenkot , a former military chief.

• Main issues: Security and accountability are powerful electoral forces after years of war. Opinion polls suggest the economy and cost of living are also leading concerns for many voters.

• Parliamentary make-up: No single party has ever won a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, or Knesset. Instead, governments are formed through alliances, which can take weeks or even months to form.

Israel’s two leading candidates have made emotionally charged stops on their election day trail.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leading challenger to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, visited the grave of his son, Gal Meir, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023. Eisenkot and his wife Hannah made a stop at the cemetery in Herzliya on his way to vote.

“Over Gal’s grave, I swore that the price he paid, he and his friends, those he knew, and those he didn’t, would not be in vain,” Eisenkot wrote about his son in Yedioth Aharonoth in April 2026, calming that promise central to his political mission. Two other nephews were killed during the war.

On Monday, the night before the vote, Netanyahu visited the Jerusalem Western Wall, as did other right-wing party leaders, traditionally placing a prayer note between the stones.

‘To the lives of IDF soldiers, our heroes, To victory over our enemies. To the success of our people, The eternity of Israel will not lie,” he said.

Families affected by the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023 have held pictures of their loved ones outside of several polling places in Israel throughout the day.

Gil Dickmann is the cousin of Carmel Gat, 39, who was kidnapped from the kibbutz of Be’eri near the Gaza border and killed in Hamas captivity. Standing outside a Tel Aviv polling station holding a picture of Gat, he told CNN he came “to remind everyone that October 7 is still here.” Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, he said, “did not admit that it was his responsibility that he was in charge of keeping us safe and secure, and he’s running again, for reelection. It’s unbelievable that he has the guts to run again.”

Outside a polling station in the coastal city of Netanya, Ruby Chen held a picture of his son Itay, a soldier killed on October 7, whose body was kidnapped to Gaza for over two years.

Early Tuesday morning, families of October 7 victims and former hostages gathered at Tel Aviv’s Hostages Square to hold a somber minute of silence at 6:29 a.m. - the exact moment the Hamas - led attacks began - before calling to vote for political accountability.

Voter turnout in Israel’s elections remains at the highest levels in more than 50 years, according to the Central Elections Committee. As of 2 p.m. local time, 44.9% of voters had cast a ballot, the committee said, the highest turnout recorded since 1973 at that hour.

A total of 3,290,480 voters out of approximately 7.3 million voted already, the committee said.

“It’s a historic high since measurement began in 1973,” said Ofer Kenig, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, “but of course we have to see whether turnout increase in all sectors and in all strongholds.”

Kenig told CNN that, from preliminary information, “In all sectors we have an increase, except for one, and a very significant one. Only in the ultra-orthodox cities, we see a decrease in voter turnout. In other segments of the Israeli society, we see an increase. Very, very cautiously we can see a higher increase in liberal strongholds rather than the Netanyahu coalition strongholds.”

Kenig cautioned that there are still hours of voting left and some groups may simply vote later in the evening.

High voter turnout poses a risk to the smaller parties running for the Knesset, putting them in danger of falling below the electoral threshold as the turnout rises. Parties need to secure 3.25% of the vote to cross the threshold; the total number of votes needed rises as overall turnout increases.

Meanwhile, voter turnout amongst the Israel Defense Forces stood at 48% as of 1 p.m. local, the military said, an increase from the 2022 election in which 44.4% had voted at the same hour.

Palestinians in Gaza have no vote in Israel’s election. But its outcome will shape their future.

More than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, with Israeli strikes a near daily occurrence, despite a nominal ceasefire agreed a year ago. Meanwhile, the humanitarian catastrophe continues to deepen, with severe food shortages, widespread displacement, and collapsing basic infrastructure.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, have both centered their election pitches on ending Hamas rule there.

But for many in the enclave, who wins the election is moot. Here’s what three people in central Gaza told CNN.

Ahed Ferwana: “The programs announced by the Israeli parties — whether parties of Netanyahu’s camp or parties of the opposition — all agree that there will not be an independent Palestinian state. They will not withdraw from the Gaza Strip and will continue military campaigns both in the Strip and even in the West Bank, as is currently seen in the city of Hebron.

“Therefore, these elections are not expected to produce significant results in favor of the Palestinian cause, especially since Eisenkot recently said frankly that he might return to war on the Gaza Strip because there is no quicker option, as he puts it. … As for Netanyahu’s camp … it has been committed to the war for more than three years.”

Musa Ubeid: “I do not count on the right, nor the left, nor anyone in Israel, because they consider our children terrorists, so how can we want or count on any party? They are two sides of the same coin.”

Tareq Abu Eweimeh: “Trump and Netanyahu have one policy, which is wars and their continuation and bloodshed. Therefore their goals are united and they are walking on one path.”

The polls in Israel’s pivotal national election – widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – are still open for about seven more hours.

Turnout in the first few hours of voting is the highest it has been in 45 years, the country’s Central Elections Committee said.

Opinion polls suggest the race will be too close to call, with Netanyahu in a tight race against centrist opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot . And many Israelis have said the choice is more consequential than ever .

Many other opposition candidates in Israel’s national elections have also already cast their votes.

In total, there are 37 parties running in the election, although most parties will fall below the threshold of votes needed to get into Israel’s parliament. Candidates can continue to campaign throughout the day, in last-minute pushes to turn out the vote.

Former Israeli Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the temporarily named Bennett 2026 party, said that it’s “a fateful day for the future of our country” as he dropped his ballot in the box. Bennett voted in the city of Ra’anana, Israel.

The leader of the Democrats party, Yair Golan, cast his ballot in the city of Rosh Haayin, Israel. “A morning of great hope. In this morning, we begin the journey of rebuilding Israel (to be) better – better for its citizens, better for its prosperity and its renewed success,” Golan said as he voted

Meanwhile in Tel Aviv, opposition leader Yair Lapid voted alongside his wife.

Former Israeli Defence Minister and leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, Avignon Lieberman, voted in the village of Nokdim, in the occupied West Bank. Calling on everyone to “come out and vote,” Lieberman said, “I am confident that tomorrow we will wake up to a new morning, one in which we can form a Zionist coalition.”

Israelis vote for party lists, not individual candidates. In a society divided by nationality, religion, ethnicity and ideology, that produces a crowded field. There are 36 parties in play.

Dozens of lists register each cycle, but only those that pass a 3.25% vote threshold win seats and enter the 120-seat Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

Polls suggest 11 to 13 parties will meet the bar; seats are allocated through a proportional representation system.

The two largest parties are Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud and Yashar, a new centrist party led by Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who has emerged as his principal challenger.

What do the polls say? The latest Channel 12 opinion poll puts Eisenkot first with 23 seats, ahead of Likud with 21, though other pollsters differ. On the pro-Netanyahu Channel 14, Likud is projected to take 30 seats and Eisenkot about 20.

In head-to-head matchups about who is better suited to be prime minister, Eisenkot has led Netanyahu by a steady margin.

But coming out as the largest party is not enough to win. A prime minister needs 61 seats to form a government, and no party has ever won that majority alone. So, election night usually settles very little. The real contest is the coalition calculus that follows, which can take days, weeks or even months.

As voters across Israel head to the polls, some of the country’s leaders have already cast their ballots and are urging people to do the same.

Gadi Eisenkot, the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in this election and head of the new Yashar party, went to the Gaza periphery to meet Gadi Mozes, one of the Israeli hostages captured during the October 7 attacks and later released by Hamas.

“I promise you that I will do everything to be worthy of your trust. That I will bring unifying leadership. That I will be prime minister of everyone – if you choose me.”

His opponents were also vocal online on Tuesday.

Defense Minister Israel Katz, a longtime Netanyahu ally, framed the election as a choice between a “decisive approach” to Israel’s security – or “a return to the policy of containment and restraint.”

President Isaac Herzog and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir both posted photos of themselves submitting their paper votes into the ballot box.

“I call on all female and male citizens of the country - we are all equal, this is our day to go, to influence and to vote,” Herzog said in a statement. “Tomorrow, we will all continue here together - we have no other country.”

Voting has begun in one of Israel’s most significant elections in its history, where voters are facing a familiar question: Should Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, stay in power?

It is the first national vote since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023 , the deadliest security failure in Israel’s history, and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran — conflicts that have mobilized much of the country and subsequently deepened Israel’s international isolation.

Here’s what’s been happening so far today:

Voter turnout is currently the highest it has been in 45 years , according to the country’s Central Elections Committee. It is the highest voter turnout since 1981, the committee said at a press conference.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – leader of the Likud party – cast his vote at a polling station in Jerusalem, calling it a “very moving and fateful moment.”

Opposition candidate and former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has also voted at a polling station in the coastal city of Herzliya, in the northern part of the Tel Aviv district. “I suggest not to get excited by Netanyahu’s scare tactics,” Eisenkot said outside the polling station.

Family members of those killed and taken hostage in the October 7 attacks gathered at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv for a minute of silence at 6:29 a.m., marking the moment when Hamas-led gunmen began the attack.

CNN’s Tal Shalev, Oren Liebermann, Lauren Kent and Kathleen Magramo contributed to this reporting.

Opposition candidate and former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has just voted at a polling station in the coastal city of Herzliya, in the northern part of the Tel Aviv district.

Eisenkot, the main rival to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has spent the rest of the morning visiting other polling locations to greet voters.

“I suggest not to get excited by Netanyahu’s scare tactics. … He does this in every election campaign,” Eisenkot said outside the polling station after casting his ballot.

His new party Yashar – “straight” in Hebrew – is considered centrist, and Eisenkot has primarily campaigned on issues that are domestic and address government accountability.

You can read CNN’s full profile of Eisenkot and his policies here .

In the prominent Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank, voters said they were focused on uniting a country that has grown more fractured and divided over the last four years.

“I hope my children will have a good place to grow up, that there will be brotherhood among us, not just wars,” Elinor Veinglas told CNN. She said she hopes “that we will remember to come together and that will be our foundation here in this country.”

Even so, Veinglas said she would only decide for whom to vote “when I see the ballots.”

Her husband, David Veinglas said he would vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rival, Gadi Eisenkot. “I believe whatever comes in the end will be fine,” he told CNN. “I hope for a united government.”

Meanwhile, Haviva, who declined to give her last name, said she prays for “the people of Israel, especially that there will be unity and that they will first find what they have in common between right and left.”

Just south of Jerusalem, Efrat is more ideologically diverse community than settlements deep in the West Bank that are aligned with far-right parties. Israeli settlements are considered illegal under International law by most of the international community and the United Nations.

Zvolon, who also declined to give his last name, said he was voting for far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich. “The people of Israel were exiled for 2,000 years living among the non-Jews. We had no government. Today we come and vote. I can say it seems my ancestors dreamed of this day,” Zvolon said.

One week before Israel’s Election Day, President Donald Trump finally gave the full-throated endorsement that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had long sought.

The president called Netanyahu a “Great Warrior Prime Minister” in a post on social media, which he said serves as his “Complete and Total Endorsement of Bibi Netanyahu.”

Trump also hinted at a possible resumption of hostilities in the unpopular war with Iran — a war the US launched alongside Israel eight months ago — saying that if the Iranians do not “change their ways, rapidly, we will soon finish the job.”

Netanyahu was quick to respond, thanking Trump for the “tremendous support and the joint work.”

Trump told Axios journalist and CNN Global Affairs analyst Barak Ravid in a brief phone interview that he had always intended to endorse Netanyahu. “I was always going to do that. I just didn’t want to do it too soon,” he said.

Trump added that they have a “good relationship” and would “continue to do well” together if Netanyahu is reelected, according to Ravid.

“It is important that Israel has a person they can count on,” Trump said.

It was an endorsement that seemed uncertain until it finally arrived and cannot mask what has become at times a rocky relationship between the two.

As soon as polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time, Israel’s main TV stations publish their exit polls. The projections trigger an explosion of chatter and conjecture, as pundits and voters alike digest the results.

Thirty years ago, exit polls pointed to a close result but, still, the winner looked clear.

Liberals and leftists who had work the next day, and could not afford to keep watching through the night, switched off their TVs comfortable their man, Shimon Peres, had won.

But overnight, as votes were counted, and exit pollsters adjusted their projections, the tide started to turn in favour of Peres’s opponent. It does not always change like that, but in 1996 it did.

And the longer the night went on, the more the tide turned.

For the Israeli left, it meant the most appalling shock when they switched their TVs and radios back on in the morning to get the news.

Likud was back in office under their new, young, leader.

“What just happened” they asked themselves. “We went to bed with Peres, we woke up with Netanyahu!”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu – leader of the Likud party – and his wife Sara Netanyahu just cast their votes at a polling station in Jerusalem. Already Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu is running for a record seventh term .

“It’s a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are impressed. … We really know what’s on the line, and because I can’t say things explicitly, I will say vote correctly,” Netanyahu said on Tuesday as he placed his vote in the ballot box. “That’s what we’re doing for the future of the State of Israel.”

Israel’s election is set to be a test of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership and of his ability to form a coalition, a professor on Israel studies told CNN.

“The key to his political longevity is that he is the master of coalition making and putting together a coalition, which can be a very complicated process. He’s shown time and again, even when he’s actually not received the largest number of seats in the parliament, he’s still been able to end up as prime minister,” said Dov Waxman, director of the UCLA Y&S Nazarian Center for Israel Studies.

For many voters, the election is a chance to make a decision who should lead the country in conflict and demand accountability over October 7 security and intelligence failures

“Although this is in many ways a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership, Israelis aren’t actually voting for or against Netanyahu or for his main rival,” Waxman told CNN’s Elex Michaelson.

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, leader of the Religious Zionist Party, has just cast his vote at a polling station in Kedumim settlement, in the occupied West Bank.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, chairman of the ultranationalist Otzma Yehudit party, also just voted in the occupied West Bank settlement of Kiryat Arba.

Smotrich and Ben Gvir – both key members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government – have drawn intense international scrutiny for their far-right policies in relation to Palestinians and Arab citizens. Both leaders have made the push to rebuild Jewish settlements in Gaza and the expansion of settlements in the occupied West Bank into central issues of their campaign .

CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this post.

Benjamin Netanyahu has already secured his record in Israeli political history: He is the longest-serving prime minister, notching up roughly 19 years across three periods in office.

In 2019, he surpassed David Ben Gurion, Israel’s founding prime minister, who was in office 13 years and 127 days.

Netanyahu, now 77, was 46 when he first became prime minister in 1996. He held the post for three years before losing power and spending a decade out of office.

In 2009 he made his first comeback, returning to the premiership for 12 consecutive years. In 2021, Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid succeeded in assembling an alternative governing coalition, but it collapsed after barely a year. Bennett served for one year and 17 days, and Lapid succeeded him for just 181 days, making them the two shortest-serving prime ministers in Israel’s history.

After a brief period in the opposition, Netanyahu made his second comeback, returning to power in December 2022 for his sixth term. His outgoing government also set a record, becoming the first Israeli government to conclude its full term in almost 40 years.

Netanyahu carries another historic distinction. He is the first sitting Israeli prime minister to stand trial for corruption while in office, a legal saga that has shaped his political alliances over the past decade and increased his reliance on far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners, with whom he formed his last coalition.

As Netanyahu seeks a seventh term, the election is once again a referendum on his leadership, but this time he also bears another historic burden. Netanyahu was the sitting prime minister on October 7, 2023, the date of the deadliest security failure in Israel’s history. He is the only top Israeli official who served that day to remain in office.

This election will determine if Netanyahu extends his record-setting tenure, or if another chapter in Israel’s political history begins.

In the first few hours of voting in Israel’s election, voter turnout is the highest it has been in 45 years, according to the country’s Central Elections Committee.

As of 10 a.m. local time, voter turnout stood at 16.68%, the committee said, higher than the turnout at the same hour four years ago, which was 15.9%. It is the highest voter turnout since 1981, the committee said at a morning press conference.

Ofer Kenig, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, said it showed that Israelis clearly viewed the elections as a pivotal moment, even as he warned it was still too early to draw broad conclusions.

“I think it’s a sign of enthusiasm, of the perception of many Israelis of very significant elections - very crucial elections,” Kenig told CNN. But he also urged caution, since the turnout wasn’t dramatically higher yet than the previous election.

“Let’s see how it will develop during the day.”

Even so, far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich tried to use the figure to drive his own voter base. In a post on X, he claimed, “The high voter turnout figure is a result of exceptional turnout rates in the Arab sector and in left-wing strongholds.”

Outside a polling station in the Jerusalem neighborhood of Katamon, signs for a diverse spectrum of parties decorated the street. From the far-right party of Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich to the left-wing party of Yair Golan, campaign activists pitched voters one last time before they entered the polling place early Tuesday morning.

Israelis last voted in an election in November 2022 and viewed this as a critical chance to decide the future direction of the country.

“We are a Zionist family who loves the country, and we want as quickly as possible to exercise the right to vote and to feel that we are part of this whole country and are doing good,” Gabi Touboul told CNN.

Shirel, who voted early to avoid the lines said: “We are taking advantage of this day because my daughters came from the corners of the country to make a change, amen!”

At a polling place near the entrance to Jerusalem, signs for Gadi Eisenkot covered fences in the area. As of Tuesday morning, only the far-right Noam party – which polls show is not expected to qualify for the Knesset – also had signs there.

Adam Maayan voted at the polling site early “in order to make a change,” he told CNN.

Family members of those killed and taken hostage on October 7 in 2023 gathered at Hostages Square in Tel Aviv for a minute of silence at 6.29 a.m, marking the moment when Hamas-led gunmen began the attack.

The families, in a statement, reiterated their demand for a state commission of inquiry on the attack and also called on Israelis to “remember the loved ones they lost and to carry their memory” when casting their ballots.

Her daughter Mappel Adam was killed at the Nova music festival, she said.

“Vote responsibility. Vote state commission of inquiry. Vote change. Vote hope.”

articles.title: MORNING GLORY: The Democrats have a 'Fanatic Four' of extremist Senate candidates
articles.summary: Democrats risk four United States Senate seats as Abdul El-Sayed, Peggy Flanagan, Troy Jackson and James Talarico struggle against centrist GOP foes.
articles.body: Despite the basic rule of politics — it takes 50% of the vote plus one to win — both parties have occasionally put forward nominees from the farther reaches of the right or from the extreme left. Those candidates have sometimes combined terrible public personalities and debate skills with policy positions far beyond the edges of mainstream politics. This year, Democrats are trying to sell four extremists to voters: Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, Peggy Flanagan in Minnesota, Troy Jackson in Maine and James Talarico in Texas. In three of those four races, Republicans have countered with nominees from the center: Mike Rogers in Michigan, Michele Tafoya in Minnesota and the incumbent in Maine, Senator Susan Collins, who, as chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, is the most powerful woman inside the Beltway and whose defeat would be an enormous "own goal" for Mainers. MORNING GLORY: FIVE SENATE RACES SHOW WHY DEMOCRATS MAY REGRET THEIR PRIMARY CHOICES The Republican Senate nominee in Texas is the state’s own attorney general, Ken Paxton, who has run and won three times in the Lone Star State. Paxton is a flawed candidate, but he will be a reliable GOP vote in the Senate and the party has rallied to him even though there are bruised feelings from the contentious primary. Republicans have indulged their base over the years, especially in 2010 when they put forward Christine O’Donnell in Delaware, Sharron Angle in Nevada and Ken Buck in Colorado, and in 2012 with the nominations of Todd Akin in Missouri and Richard Mourdock in Indiana. All five of those Republicans lost. This year, a week out from Election Day, it especially doesn’t look good for Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Troy Jackson in Maine. El-Sayed has a reflexive attitude of grievance and, in Maine, Jackson suffers in any side-by-side comparison with Susan Collins, who is a formidable political athlete. DAVID MARCUS: IN BLUE MAINE, NOBODY BELIEVES SUSAN COLLINS WILL LOSE UNTIL THEY SEE IT Talarico has seen Paxton rise and rise in the polls and the GOP has spent millions showing Texans how far out in left field Talarico plays. Talarico weirdly vanished from the campaign trail for a dozen days and blamed the flu. In Minnesota — the "bluest" of the four states — the epic fraud scandal has followed Flanagan's campaign, who has been the state’s lieutenant governor since 2019. Flanagan is matched against the political "rookie of the year" in Republican moderate Michele Tafoya, a sparkling and affable centrist. Democrats have tried to prop up their failing four fanatics by sending out Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and have pulled former President Barack Obama off Martha’s Vineyard to throw him into the breach. Trouble is "AOC," "Bernie" and "Kamala" all telegraph "wacky or worse" into the electorate’s consciousness, and the former president’s shtick was old in 2014 when he helped provoke a red wave with Republicans netting nine Senate seats and a baker’s dozen House seats. EL-SAYED’S SCATHING OBAMA CRITIQUE RESURFACES AHEAD OF JOINT CAMPAIGN RALLY El-Sayed’s campaign seems to be in free-fall as the candidate first turned argumentative, then angry, in appearances culminating last week with his interview with Fox News’ own Bret Baier. El-Sayed’s hostile and rude treatment of Baier — the quintessential gentleman of the news business — was instantly understood by anyone who saw it as an attempt to hide his record by loudly talking over Baier’s questions and deflecting to non-issues unrelated to Baier’s straightforward and brief questions. That interview may have done the candidate the most damage of the cycle as it came after Rogers had just blistered El-Sayed in their final debate. El-Sayed’s many attempts in many settings to cover up the details of his Medicare for All tax-spend-and-ration healthcare boondoggle with semantics and word puzzles left viewers wondering on what topic could they actually trust El-Sayed? Certainly not Iran or Islamist extremism, as El-Sayed’s frantic attempts to escape his past actions and statements have backfired. El-Sayed’s biggest blunder — his declaration that "hurt people hurt people" after an attack on a Michigan synagogue — has never receded in the public’s mind. Rogers, meanwhile, has methodically campaigned in traditional Democratic strongholds in and around Detroit and Pontiac and stresses his distinguished career as a federal and state legislator, FBI agent and Army officer. DAVID MARCUS: THE 5 FACTORS THAT COULD DECIDE MICHIGAN'S TIGHT AND UGLY SENATE RACE Peggy Flanagan and James Talarico simply haven’t, and apparently cannot, connect with the center of their states’ electorates. They are just "way outside the ‘40s’" where most of American politics, like most NFL games, are played. Flanagan’s campaign is mired in the swamp of the massive fraud that engulfed part of the Twin Cities’ Somali community. Talarico’s long tenure among "the woke" has haunted him throughout the campaign, as has his resting face of innocent cluelessness. DEMOCRATS WHO ‘NEVER VOTED REPUBLICAN’ BACK ROGERS OVER EL-SAYED IN RAZOR-CLOSE RACE Up in Maine, Troy Jackson got waxed by the veteran Collins in four out of four debates in all of which Jackson struggled with very basic questions about very basic issues — like the enormous difference between Medicare and Medicaid. "Oh shut up!" Jackson also grunted into a microphone on the debate stage as Collins made a joke about a debate disrupter being a Jackson supporter. Mainers are a polite lot. They also know that turning out the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee in favor of a guy who often looks like he slept outside and just woke up would be a singularly unwise trade for everyone in the state. When the Democratic Socialists of America’s ("DSA") handpicked erratic and voluble Graham Platner had to exit the Maine race, the Maine Democratic Party could have picked anyone in the state to replace him. That they chose Jackson, the third-place loser from the then just-completed Democratic gubernatorial primary, remains one of the baffling questions in a year of political surprises. The GOP is "coming home" as President Donald Trump has exhausted his own team with daily rallies and sometimes two. The cliché that "it all comes down to turnout" isn’t lost on the president who knows the hatred of the left is priced into his persona, but that getting his own voters to the polls is exactly what his rallies do. Republicans learned from their Tea Party years that candidates cannot win with their bases, but also that you can’t win with just the base. Democrats have forgotten their wilderness years of 1980 through 1993, which only ended when Bill Clinton and the Democratic Leadership Council pulled the entire party back towards the middle. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Now the DSA has put the Democrats in full "Thelma and Louise" mode as they have accelerated their party over the left cliff of national politics. The "false positive" of Mayor Mamdani’s narrow win in the New York mayoral race last year proved to be a disaster for mainstream Democrats this year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "50% plus 1" is the formula. The Democrats of 2026 forgot that recipe even as the Republicans of 2010 and 2012 did. The consequences will be revealed next Tuesday. Hugh Hewitt is a Fox News contributor and host of "The Hugh Hewitt Show" heard weekday afternoons from 3 PM to 6 PM ET on the Salem Radio Network, and simulcast on Salem News Channel. Hugh drives Americans home on the East Coast and to lunch on the West Coast on over 400 affiliates nationwide, and on all the streaming platforms where SNC can be seen. He is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel’s news roundtable, hosted by Bret Baier weekdays at 6pm ET. A son of Ohio and a graduate of Harvard College and the University of Michigan Law School, Hewitt has been a Professor of Law at Chapman University’s Fowler School of Law since 1996 where he teaches Constitutional Law. Hewitt launched his eponymous radio show from Los Angeles in 1990. Hewitt has frequently appeared on every major national news television network, hosted television shows for PBS and MSNBC, written for every major American paper, has authored a dozen books and moderated a score of Republican candidate debates, most recently the November 2023 Republican presidential debate in Miami and four Republican presidential debates in the 2015-16 cycle. Hewitt focuses his radio show and his column on the Constitution, national security, American politics and the Cleveland Browns and Guardians. Hewitt has interviewed tens of thousands of guests from Democrats Hillary Clinton and John Kerry to Republican Presidents George W. Bush and Donald Trump over his 40 years in broadcasting. This column previews the lead story that will drive his radio/ TV show today.

articles.title: Frustrated Illinois residents seek to redraw state map in bid to break free from Chicago
articles.summary: Frustrated Illinois residents in 11 counties will vote on a non-binding referendum to break away from Cook County and form a new state in November.
articles.body: Frustrated Illinois residents are pushing to break away from Chicago and form a new state, driven by what the movement’s leader calls growing resentment over the city’s influence on the rest of Illinois. Loret Newlin, director of Illinois Separation, which is leading the push to let voters weigh in on breaking away from Cook County and forming a new state, told Fox News Digital that residents outside the Chicago area are being ignored by state government and want to change that. "Our area is not taken into consideration when laws are being made," Newlin said. "There's definitely more focus on them, and the laws are centered to benefit Chicago and Cook [County]." ‘VEXIT’ MOVEMENT REIGNITES AS RED STATE INVITES DISENFRANCHISED VIRGINIANS TO ‘BEST VIRGINIA’ "There is a lot of area outside of Cook that should have been taken into consideration," she said. Newlin said that 11 counties and several townships in Illinois will vote on a non-binding referendum in November that asks residents if they'd be interested in separating from Cook County to form a new state. TOP DEMOCRAT GOVERNORS ARE HOPING TO RIDE THEIR RECORDS TO THE WHITE HOUSE. CAN THEY? The referendums are intended to gauge whether voters want to pursue forming a separate state made up of Illinois counties outside Cook County. The effort draws on a process outlined in Article IV, Section 3 of the U.S. Constitution, the same provision invoked when West Virginia became a state in 1863. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB She pointed to a proposed per-mile tax for drivers making its way through the Illinois legislature as one example of how she says state lawmakers are overlooking downstate residents. SEND US A TIP Newlin said the proposed per-mile tax, introduced by state Sen. Ram Villivalam, whose district includes part of Chicago, would disproportionately affect rural residents, farmers and truckers who lack the public transit options available in the city. "It's a long way to a lot of important things for people who live in downstate. A lot of our businesses rely on transportation. One of our biggest industries down here is truckers, farmers. And the commute to a job is usually a little farther, and we don't have the option of taking the Chicago public transit system," Newlin said. "And we tried to defeat this in 2019 and succeeded, but as typical, they won't take no for an answer." LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST Newlin also criticized Illinois' SAFE-T Act, saying she's "not happy" with the law and believes it "really benefits the criminals," and pointed to the impact it's having on Chicago. GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL The SAFE-T Act, signed into law by Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker in 2021, eliminated cash bail and established a new system for judges to determine whether defendants should be detained or released while awaiting trial. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Pritzker has opposed the idea of separation, and a spokesperson for his office previously called the movement a "stunt" that is "not going to happen," according to NBC Chicago. Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker and Villivalam for comment.

articles.title: GREGG JARRETT: In a tortured defense of Ilhan Omar, The New York Times reaches for its darkest Trump analogy
articles.summary: The New York Times editorial board compared Trump to Hitler while defending Ilhan Omar, but the fraud investigation actually began under Biden.
articles.body: Here we go again. Trump is behaving just like Hitler. On Friday, The New York Times published an editorial with the provocative headline "Trump Is Turning to an Old Tool of Authoritarian Repression." The editorial was a defense of Minn. Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar, who is under investigation for potential immigration fraud and more. GREGG JARRETT: ILHAN OMAR COULD FACE INDICTMENT, DENATURALIZATION AND DEPORTATION The Hitler defense of Rep. Omar was conjured by the editorial board of The New York Times. Insofar as name-calling goes, it’s lame. It is also an unmistakable deflection. It’s the kind of stuff kids do in the schoolyard when caught cheating in kickball. But some kids never grow up. Perhaps they just move on to a fancier playground called The New York Times. The Trump-Hitler comparison is a tired cudgel that the Times loves to trot out periodically to remind its readers that the current occupant of the Oval Office is evil. But in the newspaper’s Friday editorial, it deployed the insult in a remarkably disconnected way. The editors argue that since tyrants in history — Hitler included — used "revocation of a political opponent’s citizenship" as a "tool of authoritarian repression" that must be what President Donald Trump is doing to Omar. REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Never mind those pesky things called the law and its enforcement thereof. In fact, the Times disregards the code of federal statutes entirely, tossing them out as utterly irrelevant or meaningless. Journalists at The New York Times have done extensive reporting on the Ilhan Omar case. But the editorial board seems more interested in blaming Trump than examining the facts. In their conceit, the editors openly confess that they are little acquainted with the known facts or evidence. "We do not pretend to know whether the allegations have merit," they write while adding, "They are not the main issue." FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION Really? Are potential crimes like false statements, fraud, conspiracy and obstruction of justice of no consequence? Immaterial? Try explaining that to the roughly 6,000 federal prosecutors who spend their professional careers upholding those types of laws. What the Times is really arguing — but doesn’t have the courage to admit — is that a Democratic member of Congress should be entitled to get away with suspected crimes because a particular person they despise is president. Of course, this ignores that the original incarnation of the Omar investigation began under the presidency of Joe Biden. Again, just another pesky detail destined to be overlooked. Instead, the editorial board traduces Trump for his "affront to free speech, the rule of law and American ideals." It doesn’t get more syrupy than that. And demonstrably wrong. DEMOCRATS HAVE ‘DIRTY HANDS’ OVER COMPLAINTS ABOUT OMAR RAID WEEKS BEFORE ELECTION, EX-PROSECUTOR SAYS Let’s take free speech as an example. It is not — and never has been — a defense against false statements or fraud in immigration matters. Period. Even more obvious is how the Times editors managed to mangle "the rule of law." It is a cherished principle that dates back to the Magna Carta in 1215. It means that all people are subject to the same rules and receive equal treatment in the legal system. DEMOCRATS' FURY OVER ILHAN OMAR RAID DRAWS STINGING GOP REMINDER ABOUT RAID FROM THE PAST: ‘SET THE PRECEDENT’ But apparently the Times believes that Omar is above the law while Trump is not. That’s quite the reversal. You may recall that during the criminal investigations of Trump, the same newspaper published numerous opinion pieces and editorials that explicitly invoked the maxim that "no one is above the law." Indeed, those very words were heralded in the titles of editorials. OBAMA BACKS ILHAN OMAR AMID PROBE, ACCUSES TRUMP ADMIN OF 'APPALLING' TARGETING IN LENGTHY STATEMENT Predictably, the Times accuses Trump of trying to "silence a critic," conveniently omitting how Biden’s Department of Justice targeted his opponent with indictments. But the real kicker is how the newspaper sobs that "no naturalized citizen will be safe." That is a clever artifice. Naturalized citizens have nothing to fear if they told the truth during the application process. But those who did not are subject to the rule of law. Congress passed a statute 120 years ago revoking citizenship in cases of fraud or false statements. Elected lawmakers did that, not Trump. But how dare the president abide by his constitutional duty to enforce the law! Or so The New York Times would have you believe. The government, regardless of who is in charge, has an obligation to investigate the possibility of criminal wrongdoing whenever evidence of it arises. In our national ideal, Lady Justice is blind. It should never matter whether there is a letter "R" or "D" after an individual’s name. Someone should tell The New York Times. FEDERAL AGENTS SEIZE PHONE OF REP ILHAN OMAR IN RAID TIED TO IMMIGRATION FRAUD PROBE Omar flatly denies that she did anything wrong or violated any laws. But it cannot be missed that it was a Democratic judge in Washington, D.C., who authorized the search of her home based on sufficient evidence that probable cause existed. The evidence seized and the accompanying warrant raise serious questions. Is Omar the person she purports to be? Was her citizenship obtained through false statements or fraud? Was there a cover-up? And did she engage in a sham marriage to her brother? CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Omar did herself no favors in a recent interview when she responded to the latter question by stating, "Not to my knowledge." That cautious and qualified reply only compounded suspicion. Was it feigned ignorance? Plausible deniability? Or was it a technical or legalistic phrase to avoid lying while hiding the truth? Journalists at The New York Times have done extensive reporting on the Ilhan Omar case. But the Editorial Board seems more interested in blaming Trump than examining the facts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP So, what will those same editors do if it turns out that the congresswoman committed citizenship fraud? Will they offer a sincere mea culpa or apology for prejudging the investigation and denouncing Trump? Not likely. They will still compare him to Hitler. Because that’s the playground on which they operate. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM GREGG JARRETT

articles.title: ‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
articles.summary: The cars have gone, and so have the buses, but while retailers expect a boost, residents worry about change.
articles.body:
London, United Kingdom – “It’s magical,” says biology teacher Muneera Alfadhel from under her umbrella.

In fact, it is a characteristically rainy, grey day in London, but the weather is doing nothing to dampen her mood. She is among the first to walk down the middle of the iconic Oxford Street following its pedestrianisation.

For generations, shoppers have bustled along Oxford Street next to bikes, cars, black cabs and red double-decker buses. But on Monday, from Great Portland Street to Orchard Street, the road is now a pedestrian-only zone.

On Monday morning, by force of habit, most pedestrians are still sticking to the pavement. Mark Arbouine, a forensic scientist out for a stroll, is one of the few breaking ranks: “I saw there was no traffic today, so I thought, why not walk in the middle of the street and take advantage of it? I just think it’s great for the environment, great for shopping. It’s just so much easier to move around the street.”

This tiny strip of real estate is big business: about 1 percent of the UK’s annual gross domestic product (GDP) is generated along this 1km (0.6 miles) stretch of street. But despite its outsized importance, Oxford Street has in recent decades been hit by lower consumer spending, as well as falling rents and footfall, which is now just 57 percent of what it was in 2006, according to New West End Company, a retail trade body.

The Greater London Authority, also known as City Hall, believes pedestrianisation could, therefore, offer a lifeline.

City Hall analysis suggests the partial pedestrianisation of Oxford Street could generate more than $109m per year and support an additional 700 jobs. Following a weekend trial in October 2025, two-thirds of businesses in the area said they had higher or similar sales figures during the pedestrianisation.

This is the first step in a multi-phase regeneration project to add two public squares, 50 trees and hundreds of public seating.

Barbara Stoll, a leading campaigner on the benefits of greener, more walkable cities, was smiling as she observed the street. The air already feels cleaner, she noted.

“It’s amazing coming here this morning. Walking down the street, it was already so uplifting that the noise is considerably lower,” she said. “People are excited. I saw people coming up from the tube and looking around. Seeing that, it’s almost like children when it’s Christmas Day.

“So I think it’s absolutely wonderful, and so needed for London.”

Residents ‘haven’t really been listened to’

On Saturday, ahead of the change, not all shoppers were convinced. A French tourist said he would avoid Oxford Street altogether if buses and cabs were no longer allowed through.

“People with disabilities who cannot walk a lot – that would be really helpful if the buses move on and they don’t discontinue [them],” a shopper told Al Jazeera.

“It would be good. Sometimes you’re tired; sometimes it’s raining.”

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has been years in the making, and not without controversy.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan first tried it in 2017, following a manifesto pledge. But the plan fell apart in 2018, when Westminster Council – the local government authority responsible for Oxford Street at the time – withdrew its backing, saying residents did not support it.

Following a public consultation, Khan created the Oxford Street Development Corporation, taking responsibility for the street away from local officials and transferring it to the Greater London Authority and Transport for London.

With this second, successful attempt at pedestrianisation, doubts from local authorities have not gone away.

Residents are not being listened to, said Councillor Tim Barnes, the deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning for the City of Westminster.

“There has been a communication process with residents, but it’s been pretty much one way. Mostly, they are being told what’s going to happen to them and how it’s going to happen; what the format of the process is going to be in future. But realistically, those who know the street best haven’t really been listened to.”

He believes the economic benefits are overstated and do not consider the impact of displacing bus routes from a major road to the surrounding, smaller streets. That fear is shared by resident Nerma Cridge, who said London’s West End will become “completely unliveable, too crowded and too noisy at night”.

“We think all of this should be done in a much more productive relationship with communities,” she told Al Jazeera over the phone.

Concerns over the change will fade once residents see the real-world results in the coming months, Stoll believes.

“Examples from across Europe and the world, where such projects have already happened, prove that this only makes life better overall for local residents,” she said.

“Retail gets a boost. More people linger, more people come to the street, more people spend money in the shops, and even local shop vacancies reduce. The local air pollution significantly reduces, and as activity increases, people just take back the space.”

The Oxford Street Development Corporation will be testing and reviewing the results of the pedestrianisation in the coming months, and reviewing its findings early next year. Transitioning the rest of Oxford Street into a permanent, traffic-free public space is expected to go ahead by the end of next year.

Ahead of mayoral elections in 2028, the pedestrianisation could be one of the last major initiatives that Sadiq Khan signs off. A landmark project that will also become his legacy.

articles.title: A US judge extends a ban on further tree removal at Trump's historic Washington golf course, where more than 400 trees were cut, and orders advance notice before other irreversible work on the site
articles.summary: A US federal judge on Monday stopped President Donald Trump's administration from cutting down more trees at a historic Washington golf course, where at
articles.body: A US federal judge on Monday stopped President Donald Trump's administration from cutting down more trees at a historic Washington golf course, where at least 400 trees have already been removed as part of a planned renovation, news agencies reported. In the order, US District Judge Ana Reyes also directed the government to give 10 business days' written notice before carrying out any other work that could permanently change the site. The decision comes as Trump prepares to close the 106-year-old East Potomac Golf Course for redevelopment, despite an ongoing legal challenge.The dispute has grown since workers removed hundreds of trees over a holiday weekend, with little warning to the people challenging the project, according to the Associated Press. The DC Preservation League and two golfers took the administration to court, arguing that its plans could damage an important part of Washington's history. They also question whether the government had followed environmental laws while preparing the site for renovation.Trump, however, has made clear that he wants the work to go ahead. On October 18, he announced that the course would close for 15 months beginning November 15 and that the construction would start the following day. Those announcements came while the court was already considering whether the government should be allowed to continue work at the site.The judge had earlier ordered a temporary halt to the project until at least October 26. Her latest decision keeps restrictions in place while the lawsuit continues.How the removal of trees led to tougher restrictionsThe disagreement over East Potomac Golf Course began months before the trees were cut. In February, the DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the administration's plans, raising concerns about environmental protection and the preservation of the historic property.For much of the case, Reyes had allowed the legal proceedings to continue without stopping the government's activities. She later explained that she had preferred the two sides to resolve their differences without additional court intervention.But the removal of at least 400 trees changed the situation. The work was carried out despite assurances that the government would not take such action. During an earlier hearing, Reyes strongly criticised the administration and described what had happened as "inexcusable".The latest order places two specific limits on the project. No additional trees can be removed or damaged, and the government must provide written notice before carrying out irreversible modifications to the course or its features.These restrictions will remain in effect while the lawsuit proceeds, unless the court changes them. The wider question of whether the renovation can legally proceed has not yet been settled.Why the judge questioned the government's positionThe court proceedings have also brought attention to differences between Trump's public announcements and the position taken by government lawyers.The president has repeatedly said that the renovation will proceed. According to Reuters, Justice Department lawyers asked Reyes to disregard Trump's public statements about the renovation when considering the case.The judge questioned that argument because the statements had come from the president whose administration was responsible for the project.She also pointed to the difficulty of examining the government's position when the president's announcements appeared to differ from sworn testimony given by government employees and arguments presented by Justice Department lawyers.Reyes wrote that the dispute had become about more than the future of a golf course. In explaining her responsibility, she said, "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."The administration also tried to have Reyes removed from the case, accusing her of improper behaviour during an emergency hearing and questioning her impartiality. She rejected that request.Trump insists renovation will go aheadDespite the court's decision, Trump has not withdrawn his plans for the golf course. Speaking to reporters late Monday, he criticised Reyes and said the administration would appeal.In a subsequent social media post, he repeated that the site would close on November 15. He said the renovation was intended to improve safety, modernise the course, make it more competitive and improve its appearance. He also said the administration will appeal the court's decision.The golf course is not the only Washington landmark Trump wants to change. His administration has also proposed a large ballroom at the White House, a massive arch and a National Garden of American Heroes in West Potomac Park. These plans have also drawn legal challenges from trpreservation groups and other opponents.The organisations challenging the renovation welcomed the latest court order. Democracy Forward, which is helping represent the plaintiffs, said the decision would protect the park from further damage while the legal proceedings continue. Its president and CEO, Skye Perryman, said the group was ready to present its arguments in court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Two British men charged with helping Iran over Fairford airbase incident
articles.summary: British prosecutors said on Tuesday they had charged two British nationals under the National Security Act over an incident last month at the RAF Fairford airbase, with police saying the two were suspected of assisting Iran.
articles.body: British prosecutors said on Tuesday they had charged two British nationals under the National Security Act over an incident last month at the RAF Fairford airbase, with police saying the two were suspected of assisting Iran. RAF Fairford had been used by US B-1 bombers to carry out strikes on Iran, but they were withdrawn on security grounds shortly after five men were arrested outside the military base in southwest England in the early hours of September 27. The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) said Tuesday it had charged Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, with engaging in conduct that was likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service. Nouman Essghir, 24, was charged with one offense of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on August 22. The pair, who both live in London, will appear at Westminster Magistrate’s Court later on Tuesday. Five other men arrested in connection with the case remain on police bail. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of national counter terrorism policing in the UK, said police believed the country Abdulkarim was assisting was Iran. “We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of Mi5 (the UK’s domestic security service) said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” Taylor added. Initially the police arrested five men “on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act” and explosives offenses near the Fairford airbase that has long used by the US Air Force. The men were then released on bail, which Taylor on Tuesday acknowledged “sparked significant questions and speculation about the investigation and why that was the case.” “We know that decisions made during our investigations can sometimes appear illogical to those on the outside, but I want to make it very clear, that there will always be good reason, or rationale behind them,” he added. “Like our adversaries, our tactics vary – and may not always be obvious.” Taylor said the decision to initially release the men “led to swifter progress, better evidence and ultimately us securing the charges.” Earlier this month, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the suspected plot targeting RAF Fairford was “almost certainly directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard.” Iran has firmly rejected the accusations. US President Donald Trump praised the arrest of the men at the time, telling reporters that the US had worked with Britain and that the men arrested were planning to do “big damage” to RAF Fairford. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” Trump said. US intelligence had tracked planning by Iranian groups to target US assets at the base weeks ahead of any arrests, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter. Days after the initial arrests, the US moved all of its long-range bombers from RAF Fairford following an unspecified threat, a knowledgeable source said. At the time, Trump and Vice President JD Vance hinted that a threat against US assets had prompted the move. “I think we can say that — I mean, they didn’t fly out by accident,” Trump said. “There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy, we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy. But why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit.” Vance said the move was made “out of an abundance of caution,” suggesting it was a response to a potential threat from Iran even as he declined to detail the specific concerns.
