articles.title: Restaurants draw the line on substitutions as diners push menu limits
articles.summary: Food allergies and dietary restrictions aside, chefs say excessive substitutions strip dishes of authentic flavor and slow down kitchen operations.
articles.body: Making substitutions at restaurants has become commonplace, but some chefs and restaurant owners are pushing back against requests they say can disrupt kitchen operations and take away from the intended dining experience. The growing debate has also raised questions about restaurant etiquette, with experts warning that excessive modifications can cross the line from reasonable requests into entitlement. Lom Wong, a Thai restaurant in Phoenix, Arizona, recently took a stance against substitutions after seeing an increase in modification requests following its recognition in the 2026 Michelin Guide Southwest. WHY RESTAURANT SERVERS CLEAR YOUR PLATE BEFORE EVERYONE FINISHES EATING Restaurant industry veteran Robert Mahon and national etiquette expert Diane Gottsman told Fox News Digital that while some substitutions are reasonable, excessive requests can create challenges for restaurants and their staff. In a post on Instagram, Lom Wong reminded diners that the restaurant serves "village Thai food" and does not follow traditional European-style coursing methods. "We'll take your whole order at once. Your dishes will come out when they're ready," the post said. The restaurant also asked guests not to expect it to "change or conform to someone else's idea of what an award-winning restaurant should be." RESTAURANTS LOCK UP CUSTOMERS' PHONES AS DEVICES BECOME THE 'NEW CIGARETTES' "We also don't make substitutions simply to make a dish more familiar," the post said. "These recipes were shared with us by our families or by the communities we work with. We respect those recipes and the people who entrusted them to us." The post drew largely supportive reactions, with some commenters praising the restaurant for standing by its approach. "The customer is NOT always right. When you come into someone else's house, you show respect and manners," one Instagram user wrote, noting that this includes eating what's on the menu. Not everyone agreed, however. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Sounds good in general but no one wants their dessert before their meal or starter after their entree, and it's crazy to say you can't decide you're hungry for more after initially ordering," one commenter wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to Lom Wong for comment. Excessive substitutions can also undermine the flavors chefs intended diners to experience, Mahon said. Chefs "create these dishes on the menu with all these different amazing flavors so the customer can experience them all at once," Mahon, director of operations for the New York-based Mahon Hospitality Group, told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "However, once you start modifying, the true authentic flavor that was originally meant to be for the dish is not there anymore," he added. "At the end of the day, we're trying to do what's best for the customer and please them to a certain degree," Mahon said. Sometimes, however, it's simply not feasible to accommodate every substitution request while running a restaurant at full capacity and providing the best service possible, Mahon said. Allergies and dietary restrictions are taken seriously and accommodated to the best of a restaurant's ability, Mahon said, but unnecessary modifications can lead to longer wait times, especially if everyone at a table makes changes to their orders. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Excessive substitution requests can also cross the line into poor dining etiquette. "If it's something minor like asking to remove the tomatoes on top of the piece of protein, for example, easy enough. But when you are completely changing up the order, that comes across as entitlement," Gottsman, founder of the Protocol School of Texas, told Fox News Digital. If a dish is "something that you really dislike, you should keep your opinions to yourself because it's offensive," she said, adding that, "if it's on their menu, it means that they think that it's important." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For diners with allergies or dietary restrictions, Gottsman said the key is "asking politely, doing it respectfully and not overburdening the wait staff or the chef."

articles.title: Whose side are we on? Trump’s Ukraine policy is baffling.
articles.summary: The tilt toward Russia makes no sense.
articles.body:
President Trump’s Ukraine policy has been, as Winston Churchill famously said of Russia, “a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma.” In 2025, he humiliated Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky in the Oval Office. He also gave Russian strongman Vladimir Putin the red-carpet treatment , ended direct American economic and military aid to Ukraine and pushed absurd peace plans that only appease Russian aggression.

The tilt toward Russia makes no sense . Speculation runs wild. Is Trump is afraid of Putin? Does Putin have blackmail material on him? Is he a Russian asset?

I think of a line often attributed to Churchill: “You were given the choice between war and dishonor. You chose dishonor, and you will have war.”

In the days since he last spoke to Putin by telephone, Trump has announced a sanctions waiver for Russian diesel supplies to the global market. He may have been involved in throttling Ukraine’s access to vital battlefield satellite systems. He put sweeping new sanctions against Russian on hold , called for Zelensky’s ouster and blocked vital supplies to Ukraine of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles both from the U.S. and European governments .

The sanctions waiver lets Russia sell diesel on the global market , and gives Putin extra cash for his war on Ukraine.

But as far as global diesel supplies go, the limiting factor remains the Iran War and the Strait of Hormuz . The Russian deal’s impact on domestic fuel prices will be minimal, and the upside impact on Russia’s economy significant.

Trump waived the sanctions, which he said was “in the national interests of the United States,” just before they would have become effective. He did not explain why or what those interests were. The sanctions were intended to squeeze Russia’s finances for its war against Ukraine. The waiver was a gift to Putin that he did not deserve.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) made no bones about his disgust: “Trump’s latest surrender to Putin again betrays our Ukrainian partners and defies clear congressional intent of legislation designed to punish Russia for its illegal war of aggression.”

Inexplicably, Trump appears to have made good on his threats to restrict Ukraine’s access to intelligence and its use of Starlink, including the satellite service’s military version. Ukraine relies on two satellite systems related to Elon Musk’s SpaceX. One is Starlink, which handles communications, defensive drones and coordinating ground forces. The other is Starshield, used for offensive purposes and controlled by the U.S. government.

Although Trump declared he had arranged an “ energy ceasefire ,” on Oct. 14, Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 drones against energy and civilian targets in Ukraine. Ukraine received no intelligence warning from the U.S. Ukrainian operators, without Starlink, found they could not control drones at speeds above 100 mph.

Russia’s salvo was one of the largest attacks of the war , killing at least six Ukrainians and leaving at least 600,000 without power. Someone had obviously tipped off the Kremlin about the window of opportunity.

The sequence of events had a flavor that could have come from the pen of Bret Harte, where three play poker: One is shot, and the two survivors blame each other. Musk has been critical of Zelensky’s war against Russia. It appeared at first blush that he deliberately sabotaged Ukrainian military operations while they were underway, in defiance of American national security policy. But Musk blamed Trump: “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately” the president, he wrote.

Trump said that neither he nor Musk had caused the limitations: “In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down, from what I understood.” About Musk’s possible role, Trump said , “it wasn’t me, and it wasn’t Elon, as I understand.” But Reuters had reported that the order to limit Starshield for Ukraine came from inside the White House.

According to sources familiar with the discussions, it was Musk who had approached Trump with the idea of slowing down the systems in Ukraine, and Trump agreed. One source said Musk “tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the U.S. administration that did it.” So, whodunit? The source said: “The reality is that they were both in it.” Ultimately, American officials blamed Musk for the restriction.

Zelensky said the speed and usage restrictions had been deliberately imposed on Starshield. “This is a planned operation.” The Ukrainian leader suggested that the restrictions, which began overnight on Oct. 13, were in place until Saturday, when he announced that operations were back to normal. A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has demanded an investigation into the disruptions .

Whose side are we on in Ukraine? Trump has left us mystified.

James D. Zirin is a former federal prosecutor in the Southern District of New York and a published legal analyst.

articles.title: Ebola cases in DR Congo surpass 10,000 in fastest-growing outbreak
articles.summary: Nearly half of the people confirmed to have the virus have died in DRC’s fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.
articles.body:
Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have surpassed 10,000 as the outbreak continues to spread across the country and beyond its borders.

Government data released on Tuesday put confirmed cases at 10,060 and deaths at 4,887.

It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in the country’s history and nearly half of the 10,060 confirmed to have the virus have died, according to data from the DRC’s Ministry of Public Health. That also makes it the deadliest outbreak of the disease in the country’s history.

With cases also mounting outside the DRC, the wider outbreak is also the second-largest and second-deadliest on record, trailing only the 2014-2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 infected and more than 11,000 dead within two years.

About 80 percent of new cases are coming from outside the chains of transmission that health authorities are monitoring.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has said at least 95 percent of cases must come from the known contacts of infected people for the outbreak to be considered under control.

The outbreak, declared on May 15, is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare Ebola strain for which no vaccine or treatment has been approved. On Friday, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that the first clinical trial for a vaccine had been rolled out.

Five months into the outbreak, responders in the DRC say some treatment centres are overwhelmed, while remote and newly affected areas are short of medical supplies and health workers.

Cases have been recorded in 66 health zones across eight provinces, up from just three in the first days.

Many teams lack adequate vehicles and struggle to persuade families to hand over the sick for treatment and the dead for safe burial. At least half of those who have died were never admitted for treatment.

The outbreak has disrupted routine care such as childhood vaccinations, and maternal deaths doubled in some provinces soon after it was declared.

Strikes over delayed or unpaid wages are common. Last week, Ebola responders in Nia Nia, Ituri province, stopped work over bonuses owed since late August.

Health workers have also come under attack amid public mistrust and frustration with the government’s response.

On Saturday, assailants killed a nurse and seriously injured a colleague as the two responded to a suspected Ebola case in Bafwasende, Tshopo province, the WHO said.

“Everyone working to protect communities from this deadly disease must be able to work in dignity and safety,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.

Last month, Marie-Celestin Karondwa, a local politician, was fatally beaten after defending the Ebola response on the radio, his party said.

The virus has had a wider cross-border reach than any earlier Ebola epidemic. Governments and international organisations have worked to contain cross-border infections.

In neighbouring Uganda, Health Minister Chris Baryomunsi announced on Sunday that citizens returning from the DRC must quarantine for 21 days at their own expense as a precautionary measure.

The country’s officials have said there are no active infections in the country after recording 20 cases – mostly imported from the DRC – and two deaths over the summer.

Swiss authorities, however, have said a woman married to a Swiss diplomat was infected during a September visit to Uganda.

Last week, she was diagnosed with Ebola while visiting Nigeria – making it the fourth African country impacted by the outbreak. Nigerian officials have responded by instituting heightened screening for the disease at airports. On Monday, the patient was evacuated to Switzerland for treatment.

In Kenya, confirmed infections rose rapidly in October. Twenty contacts of the country’s first patient were released from a mandatory quarantine on Monday after 21 days, while 98 remain under monitoring, the WHO said. Kenya’s tally has since risen to nine confirmed cases, two of them fatal.

articles.title: Two California neighbours settled a fight over 38 ficus trees with a $78,500 payment and 19 trees removed; years later, roots invaded again, and a 2026 appeals court upheld an order to remove the remaining 19 trees
articles.summary: A long legal fight between two California neighbours over invasive tree roots has ended in state court, with a judge ordering the complete removal of a
articles.body: A long legal fight between two California neighbours over invasive tree roots has ended in state court, with a judge ordering the complete removal of a boundary hedge after years of failed attempts to reach a solution. The Fourth District Court of Appeal, Division One, upheld a lower court ruling that ordered the property owner to remove the remaining 19 ficus trees along the shared property line. The roots had continued to spread despite an earlier out-of-court settlement. The dispute began over a row of 38 ficus trees planted along the boundary between two neighbouring homes in Southern California. The fast-growing trees, often used to create privacy screens, developed large underground root systems that spread into the neighbouring yard. The roots damaged landscaping and threatened nearby structures.Financial settlement and initial compromiseTo settle the original dispute without a lengthy court battle, the two neighbours reached a formal agreement. Under the terms, the owner of the trees paid $78,500 (£60,300) to compensate the neighbour for damage caused by the roots. As part of the same agreement, both parties decided to remove exactly half of the row. A total of 19 of the 38 ficus trees were cut down to reduce the spread of the roots, while leaving part of the hedge in place to provide some privacy. However, removing only half the trees did not solve the underlying problem. Over the following years, the roots of the remaining 19 trees continued to grow and spread. New roots crossed the property line and entered the neighbouring yard again.Further root intrusion prompts court orderWith the roots continuing to cause problems, the affected neighbour returned to court to seek a lasting solution. Evidence presented during the case showed that the remaining 19 trees were still sending invasive roots across the boundary. The roots caused further property damage despite the earlier payment and partial removal of the trees. The trial court ruled in favour of the neighbour who had complained. It issued an order requiring the tree owner to remove all 19 remaining ficus trees. The tree owner then appealed the decision, challenging the order to cut down the rest of the hedge.Court of appeal upholds final removalIn an unpublished opinion in case number D085598, Armendariz v. Renfro, the California Fourth District Court of Appeal, Division One, upheld the trial court's decision in full. The appeals court found that the trial court had the authority to order the complete removal of the remaining trees. The court noted that the earlier financial settlement and partial removal had failed to stop the roots from spreading across the property line. articles.title: Ex-Britain First leader arrested in HMO attacks investigation
articles.summary: Ashlea Simon says she was arrested at Manchester Airport in connection with her identifying HMOs.
articles.body:
The former co-leader of the far-right Britain First party has said she was arrested as part of an investigation into attacks on houses in multiple occupation (HMOs).

In a post on X, Ashlea Simon said she had been held at Manchester Airport after "returning from a family holiday".

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) said a 37-year-old woman had been arrested on suspicion of "conspiracy to cause criminal damage", following a spate of incidents in which HMOs were vandalised across the Greater Manchester region.

Simon, who said in her post that she "hasn't committed a crime in her life", was approached for comment by the Local Democracy Reporting Service (LDRS).

In the post, Simon said she believed the arrest was linked to a series of videos she has made since July.

In them, she claimed to identify several HMOs in her hometown of Walkden, Salford.

In a previous video shared by Simon in recent days, she said police had "raided" her home while she was on holiday and she was aware of an "arrest warrant".

Simon left Britain First two years ago, and is now the leader of a "pro-English" activism group.

Police are investigating about 50 incidents in which HMOs and family homes have been vandalised and cars targeted.

In one incident, a pig's head was left outside a home.

Five men have been arrested on suspicion of causing criminal damage and conspiracy to cause criminal damage as part of the investigation, along with a 13-year-old boy.

On Friday, Ch Supt Marcus Noden said officers "suspect vulnerable people are being exploited and paid to damage buildings they believe are HMOs".

"Some of those being exploited are believed to be children and this is just one line of enquiry that we are pursuing," he added.

articles.title: Mysterious Roman fort discovered in remote area could prove ancient legend has roots in reality
articles.summary: Mark Merrony, an archaeologist at Oxford, told Fox News Digital the Pembrokeshire Roman fort could have held 1,000 auxiliary soldiers, rivaling garrisons on Hadrian's Wall.
articles.body: An ancient Roman fort discovered in a remote part of Wales could help unravel a centuries-old legend about a Roman emperor — and may have accommodated as many as 1,000 soldiers, the archaeologist behind the discovery told Fox News Digital. The fort, located near Frenni Fawr in Pembrokeshire, was the subject of an October announcement by Wolfson College, Oxford, following recent excavations at the site. Mark Merrony, a fellow at Wolfson College, Oxford, and editor-in-chief of Antiqvvs, an archaeology magazine, first identified the fort using satellite imagery in 2024. AMERICA'S LITTLE-KNOWN CASTLES, DISPLAYING ‘RAW POWER,’ ARE HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT More recent excavations uncovered two Roman coins from the late fourth century, suggesting activity at the site may have continued into the period when Emperor Magnus Maximus ruled Britain from 383 to 388 A.D. Merrony, who described the fort's location as being in the "middle of nowhere," told Fox News Digital the site could have accommodated significantly more soldiers than he initially estimated. "I've been saying 500 troops, but actually it's bigger than the housesteads on Hadrian's Wall, which held 1,000 troops," he said. "So it could have held up to 1,000 auxiliary Roman soldiers." ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MASSIVE ANCIENT SITE DURING RAIL PROJECT, INCLUDING RARE ROMAN FIND Excavations also uncovered numerous Roman artifacts, including ceramic roofing tiles and what Merrony believes could be floor tiles or materials used for underfloor heating. Despite the attention surrounding the fourth-century coins, Merrony believes the fort itself is more significant. "I think the presence of the site is more important than the coins because it was almost certainly founded in the 1st century," he said. The possible connection to Maximus stems from the "Mabinogion," a medieval collection of Welsh tales and legends that also features King Arthur. HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR One story recounts the Roman emperor establishing a military camp near Frenni Fawr. Merrony told Fox News Digital he identified the fort while tracing the Roman road network, rather than deliberately searching for evidence of the legend. "The question is, is the ‘Mabinogion’ correct? And I suspect it is." After discovering the fort roughly two miles from the hill's summit, he found no other known Roman sites nearby — leading him to suspect the fort could be the one described in the "Mabinogion." "And I put two and two together, and I thought the question is not whether this is the site. The question is, is the ‘Mabinogion’ correct? And I suspect it is," Merrony said. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER He cited the story's "very strong historical underpinning," suggesting that Roman soldiers may have traveled through the area during the late Roman period, possibly under Magnus Maximus himself. Though the discovery does not establish that the emperor visited the fort, Merrony believes the legend may preserve the memory of an actual historical event. He said he wasn't surprised that the medieval tale might contain elements of historical truth. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "I think it's often the case with mythology that it's based on something," Merrony told Fox News Digital, adding that it likely spread through oral tradition before being written down. Merrony also theorized that Maximus may have visited the region in response to incursions by Irish groups during the fourth century, before departing Britain for continental Europe. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Merrony, whose upcoming book, "Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus," explores the history of Rome's emperors, also pointed to a possible Roman road running alongside the fort. He believes the road could be part of a previously unidentified major route through Wales, although further archaeological investigation is needed. Merrony also said an aqueduct feeding the fort remains to be investigated, with additional excavations planned for 2027. Looking ahead, Merrony said his team plans to widen two excavation trenches over two buildings at the site. In one trench, researchers spotted what appeared to be a collapsed building. It's going to be really exciting," he said.

articles.title: Norway and Finland hold rare call with Putin to discuss ending war
articles.summary: This is the first time European leaders have had direct communication with Russia's president in more than a year.
articles.body:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - a rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.

The aim was looking at "future negotiations to help to end the war" in Ukraine, the offices of President Alexander Stubb and Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said. Their initiative was not on behalf of "Europe as a whole".

After the call, Putin said "confrontational" EU and Nato policies were prolonging the war which began when Russia launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has spoken to the two Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. Last week, Zelensky met them as well as US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo.

The Ukrainian leader said he was grateful for the "active support" of his Finnish and Norwegian counterparts.

Tuesday's 90-minute phone call was held from the Finnish capital Helsinki, and showed "big differences in views", Støre said.

Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the call to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.

The call was "frank and substantive", Stubb said, explaining that the war's outcome will "have a direct impact on our and the broader European security".

Støre added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."

The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.

He - like Stubb and Støre - had agreed to continue their direct phone communication, the statement added.

Rosenberg: Russia agrees to Ukraine talks but sees little to talk about in new peace push

Støre said all their allies had been informed of the call ahead of time.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "very sceptical" of Tuesday's dialogue, telling Danish broadcaster DR, it had not been "co-ordinated with any of the rest of us".

Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Stubb had informed him that Europe's position on the upcoming talks in the United Arab Emirates, was "moderately optimistic".

Relations between the US, Ukraine and its European allies have been souring since US President Donald Trump agreed to lift some sanctions from Russia - allowing it to export oil to the US.

But last week, Stubb, Støre and Zelesnky met with Witkoff in the Norwegian capital, before the US special envoy travelled on to St Petersburg to meet Putin.

Following the talks, Ukraine, Russia and the US agreed to resume three-way negotiations that Russia had stopped for months.

After speaking to the two Nordic leaders, Zelensky said part of their discussions with Putin had centred on November's trilateral talks to be held in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky said he had discussed with them "various formats for our engagement with partners in Europe that could be useful in further supporting diplomacy, our defense, and our shared security".

Stubb and Støre are the first European leaders to contact Putin since French President Emmanuel Macron's conversation with him in July 2025.

As the US administration's position on Russia has softened, several European leaders have said Europe should be trying to establish direct contacts with the Kremlin.

Moscow regularly mocks European leaders and accuses the European Union of prolonging the war by supplying Ukraine with weapons.

But last weekend, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said having a European negotiator at the peace talks table would be "good".

articles.title: Florida police called to youth soccer game after alleged dispute involving 3-year-old player
articles.summary: It was supposed to be a fun weekend soccer game for children.
articles.body: It was supposed to be a fun weekend soccer game for children. Instead, an alleged dispute involving a 3-year-old player ended with police being called to a Florida park, footage of which has since gone viral online and sparked outrage. The Winter Park Police Department said in a statement that officers responded to a call from a soccer league official alleging a disturbance involving the child’s parents. Nevada Pierre’s parents insist the 3-year-old was “scorned” for playing too well at a game Saturday, according to the police report. But the game’s sports league director argued the child was removed “due to behavior” and said his “unruly parents” were “upset with their son’s playing time,” the police report said. Officers determined the “incident was a civil matter between those parties and not criminal. No one was arrested, trespassed, or forced to leave the park,” police added in a statement. “The league requested the family leave and offered to refund the league cost to the family,” police said Monday. “The family stated the game was over and they were leaving.” “The family was cooperative with the officers,” police added. The dispute, however, has long since left the soccer field, and video footage of young Pierre weaving between players and scoring goals has gone viral online, along with the call to police as the incident has gained steam. High-profile children’s educator and entertainer Ms. Rachel labeled the incident “sick.” “The police were called on a 3-year-old Black boy because he’s too good at soccer. He was kicked out of the league. The cops showed up at the game,” Ms. Rachel wrote online. “I’m LIVID!” She then invited Pierre onto her popular children’s show to “share his amazing skills.” “I need my sports people to show up!!! This is racist, sick, traumatizing and disgusting,” Ms. Rachel said. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump also posted on X decrying the incident. “A 3-year-old was allegedly removed from a youth soccer league because he was too good,” Crump wrote. “If this child was punished for excelling, what message does that send to every young athlete?!” Former professional football quarterback Robert Griffin III also expressed his outrage. “Calling the cops on a 3-year-old is crazy,” he said, labeling Pierre a “soccer phenom.” He added, “Punishing a 3-year-old child for being too good at a sport is ridiculous.” i9 Sports, the organization behind the youth soccer program, said in a statement to NBC News that it is reviewing the incident. “We are aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously,” the group said, adding that it “reached out to the family and have begun a review that includes speaking with those involved.” “The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us,” the program added. In the 911 dispatch call obtained by NBC News, the local league official is heard saying, “I just have an unruly parent here,” referring to Pierre’s mother as “just really really disruptive.” He then accused her of “following me around and calling me names and in front of this whole bunch of people.” In an interview with ABC News, Pierre’s mother, Martasia Griffin, said that she merely “spoke up” for her son and that the family was left feeling “embarrassed” after police were called to the game. In videos shared on Pierre’s official Instagram page, his parents show snippets of him playing and say the toddler scored 10 goals at the weekend game, despite being taken off early. “The league kicked Nevada out because every week no one could take the ball from him some of the parents for the other team didn’t feel that it was fair, mind you he is a 3 year old playing with 5 years old,” a statement alongside a video on his page said.

articles.title: Iranians brace for renewed attacks after Israeli, US elections
articles.summary: The US and Israel have teased strikes around their elections, particularly against Iran’s civilian infrastructure.
articles.body:
Israelis have gone to the polls to decide whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power. On November 3, midterm elections in the United States will take place and likely impact President Donald Trump’s final years in office.

Many Iranians are watching both elections closely, knowing that the way Israelis and Americans vote could have serious consequences for their future. Since Israel and the US launched an unprovoked war on Iran on February 28, Iranians have experienced bombings, a blockade and sanctions.

But despite a sharp decrease in US and Israeli attacks since a memorandum of understanding was reached between Washington and Tehran in June, the threat of war has re-emerged. Many political commentators believe that the US and Israel could restart the war after the elections, and Iranians are anticipating further strikes.

“I haven’t followed the Israeli election very closely. But I think there will be more fighting whether Netanyahu wins or Eisenkot or someone else,” 37-year-old Tehran resident Sajad told Al Jazeera, asking to remain anonymous due to security reasons.

He believes that the rhetoric of Israeli officials signals that their ambition in the war is still for the overthrow of the Islamic Republic, which has controlled Iran since a 1979 revolution.

This has gained some support from Iranians inside and outside the country, who are opposed to the government. But cyber intelligence operations by both Israel and Iran make it difficult to accurately gauge online reactions to the prospect of Netanyahu winning another election.

Iranian authorities have described pro-Israeli Iranians as “homeland sellers” and continue to severely punish any perceived cooperation with Israel based on national security charges.

They also fully blame the US and Israel for Iran’s nationwide protests in January, during which thousands of civilians are believed to have been killed. The United Nations says Iranian security forces committed crimes against humanity while cracking down on the protests.

Shayan, a 32-year-old Tehran resident, said he believes that any Iranians who might have hoped for the overthrow of the government at the start of the war are disillusioned after witnessing US and Israeli conduct since then, with thousands of civilians killed and the US blockade and sanctions hitting most people’s incomes.

“I think some people’s viewpoints adjusted after some of the comments from the US and Israel, and after they bombed infrastructure that we need to live, like oil and gas, power and steel,” he told Al Jazeera.

“I think most Iranians don’t have a choice in the matter, but want some stability and peace.”

President Trump has threatened to bring about the “death of a civilisation” in Iran and suggested the country’s map may look different after the war.

He has also repeatedly threatened to launch more major strikes against Iran’s power plants, bridges and other civilian infrastructure if hostilities resume. US media report that the country’s military is prepared to attack over the coming days if an order is given.

The other option Trump has threatened is prolonging a naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in place since July, which has stopped the country’s oil exports and significantly disrupted trade. Together with some of the most stringent sanctions imposed against any country, the US measures have made Iranians poorer and more isolated from the international community.

The Netanyahu government has also threatened to strike Iranian infrastructure again, including energy facilities. Defence Minister Israel Katz has repeatedly said in recent months that he wants to send Iran “back into the Stone Age”.

His election opponents and other prominent opposition figures, including Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan, have all cheered the US-Israeli attacks on Iran both during the current war and during last year’s 12-day war.

They have also been united in wanting to remove Iran’s enriched uranium stockpiles from Iran and dismantle the country’s nuclear programme. Another goal is eliminating the Tehran-backed “axis of resistance” of armed forces who oppose Israel and the US across the region.

Israeli politicians, both the government and opposition, are generally united on the war aims of overthrowing the Iranian establishment, but differ on the method.

Eisenkot, for instance, has supported Netanyahu’s military strikes against Iran and praised Trump’s decision to launch attacks as courageous. But he also says that military operations cannot realistically overthrow the Islamic Republic, and that change must come from Iranians themselves.

Some Iranians have been mentally preparing themselves for conflict when the elections end.

Some Iranians said they have established groups with friends living in different parts of the country to warn each other of imminent strikes if they hear fighter jets flying overhead.

Some of the groups are in domestic messaging apps or over text message since Iranian authorities have said they will impose more internet and communication shutdowns if deemed necessary.

“In all seriousness, 90 million people have our eyes to the sky to see when there will be war. Damn this life we’ve lived,” a user named Ali wrote on X.

articles.title: Wirral parents who killed their baby have sentences increased
articles.summary: Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, murdered their baby, Miguel in 2024.
articles.body:
A couple who "fatally battered" their three-month-old son have had their "unduly lenient" sentences for murder increased.

Klevi Pirjani, 38, and 35-year-old Nivalda Pirjani, from Wirral, Merseyside, were sentenced in April to a minimum of 19 years and 15 years in April over the death of their son, 13-week-old Miguel.

The Court of Appeal has now increased Klevi Pirjani's sentence to 21 years and six months, while Nivalda Pirjani will have to serve 17 years and nine months.

Miguel was taken to Alder Hey children's hospital in November 2024. He had severe head injuries and died five days after being admitted.

Miguel was found to have suffered 41 separate bone fractures in at least four separate incidents.

The Attorney General, Ellie Reeves, referred their sentences to the Court of Appeal, with barristers for the government arguing that the original sentences did not "meet the justice of this terrible case".

Lord Justice Jeremy Baker, sitting with Mr Justice Goose and Mr Justice Hilliard, said the pair subjected their son to "routine" assaults which increased in severity, and culminated in his "particularly callous" murder.

He said: "We take the view that the resulting sentences significantly underestimated the aggravating factors, to the extent that not only do we consider that the minimum terms were unduly lenient, but that we should set them aside."

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, for the Attorney General, said in written submissions that Miguel's death was caused by an assault by his parents on 24 November 2024, which involved "a heavy blow, or series of blows, to the right side of his head".

Paramedics arrived two minutes after his parents called 999 following Miguel suffering a cardiac arrest at their home in Percy Road, Seacombe, Merseyside, but he never regained consciousness and was pronounced dead five days later.

Emlyn Jones said that while the boy was in hospital, a "wider picture of long-standing physical abuse emerged", including the discovery of multiple fractured ribs, fractured legs and a fractured sternum suffered across several incidents before the fatal attack.

He also said that while it could not be ascertained whether Klevi Pirjani or Nivalda Pirjani inflicted the fatal violence, "whichever it was, they did so with the encouragement of their partner".

Sentencing them in March, Mr Justice Andrew Baker said the pair were "in this together, encouraging each other" to attack their "defenceless" son.

He said that who "fatally battered" the infant "remains the guilty secret of a warped relationship, in which you came first for each other to an unnatural degree".

Rupert Bowers KC, for Nivalda Pirjani, acknowledged in court that "of course" her sentence was lenient, but that the sentencing judge "considered all of the factors".

He said: "There is nothing that would indicate that the sentences he passed are beyond the ambit of reasonableness, or an error of principle, so that this court should interfere with his exercise of discretion, having heard all the evidence."

Sarah Vine KC, for Klevi Pirjani, also said her client's sentence was "undoubtedly lenient, but not unduly, and leniency in itself is not a vice".

Klevi and Nivalda Pirjani, watching proceedings from HMP Wakefield in Yorkshire and HMP Styal in Cheshire respectively, showed no reaction as their sentences were increased.

articles.title: Trump’s sanctions against the International Criminal Court undermine justice
articles.summary: The United States is not simply declining to uphold international law; it is imposing costs on others for attempting to uphold it.
articles.body:
I was in Dubrovnik, Croatia, at a workshop focused on war crimes prevention, when we received the news that Navi Pillay had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her lifelong dedication to international law and accountability for war crimes.

Our celebration was short-lived. The same day, the Trump administration announced sweeping sanctions against the International Criminal Court.

The contrast was striking. Whereas the Nobel committee recognized Pillay’s achievements and the importance of international law, Washington escalated its assault on an institution that issued arrest warrants against both Israeli and Hamas leaders for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Trump himself later made clear the purpose of the move. When Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed the decision, Trump interrupted him: “ He is trying to defend [Benjamin Netanyahu]⁠ and various other people.”

These sanctions expose a deeper pattern: an administration willing to act unilaterally abroad, then scramble to manage the consequences of its own decisions, compounding crises rather than resolving them. The administration is not only shielding allies from scrutiny. Its determination to shield American actions from international accountability also raises concerns about scrutiny of its own actions — in the war on Iran, in extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and beyond.

These sanctions are not a symbolic gesture. The court relies on banks, payment systems, technology providers and commercial services. Restrictions jeopardize staff payments, secure systems, evidence preservation and investigations.

The implications for victims and witnesses are also direct and substantial. International criminal investigations depend on gathering and protecting sensitive testimony and ensuring survivors can participate without exposing themselves to further danger. Disrupting those functions would affect the people who depend on the court.

French Judge Nicolas Guillou, sanctioned in 2025, described how his bank restricted payment services and European institutions struggled to reimburse his travel expenses. The disruption extended to digital services. Fearing U.S. sanctions, institutions may avoid transactions even when they are legally permitted.

The International Criminal Court has no police force. It depends on member states to cooperate with investigations and execute arrest warrants — including those against Netanyahu and Vladimir Putin. Sanctions do not invalidate warrants but can compound obstacles to enforcement. The U.S. is not simply declining to uphold international law — it is imposing costs on others for attempting to uphold it.

On the same day that he sanctioned the International Criminal Court, Trump announced a new arrangement for Russia to supply diesel to international markets — including the U.S. Although it is intended to relieve soaring energy prices aggravated by the U.S. war with Iran, this move could generate revenue for Putin’s war in Ukraine. The message was appallingly clear — the U.S. government is willing to work with alleged international war criminals even as it targets those seeking to hold them accountable.

These choices erode leverage, credibility and the capacity to manage shared threats. Freedom from constraints does not necessarily mean greater influence. Weakening institutions does not end crises. The administration is not simply failing to extinguish crises — its responses are spreading their consequences across regions, economies and institutions.

To check Trump’s recklessness, other nations can and should respond strongly. The European Parliament has just awarded its 2026 prize for Freedom of Thought to the International Criminal Court and its officials. It is a good gesture, and one that should be backed up by more concrete action.

Guillou has called on the European Union to invoke its blocking statute , designed to protect European operators from the extraterritorial effects of foreign sanctions. It could extend protections against the U.S. measures targeting the court, prohibit covered European companies and financial institutions from complying with specified restrictions and provide remedies for those harmed.

The blocking statute cannot fully erase exposure to U.S. jurisdiction. But it would establish that European governments will not allow American economic coercion to dictate whether an international court they established can function.

The European Commission has considered this option, and France has indicated its readiness to use the mechanism. But those commitments need implementation.

In the U.S., members of Congress should unequivocally condemn and reverse the sanctions, including previous designations targeting the court’s judges and prosecutors. They must scrutinize the administration’s use of financial and security leverage to pressure governments fulfilling their international legal obligations.

When the U.S. acts as an international bully and an enforcer on behalf of leaders like Netanyahu and Putin, who are wanted for war crimes, it has a massive chilling effect that takes aim at fundamental hopes for international peace, justice and coexistence.

Dubrovnik’s Old Town is now bustling with life after enduring siege, bombardment and war crimes during the 1991-1992 war ⁠ in the former Yugoslavia. International tribunals prosecuted those responsible for war crimes there and elsewhere, demonstrating that the institutions now under attack by Trump have real purpose.

We have made progress in building mechanisms to prevent atrocities and pursue justice, but that progress is neither inevitable nor irreversible. We have seen time and again that a world in which the most powerful can do whatever they want, regardless of damage or destruction, is one in which all people are vulnerable.

Trump’s attempts to dismantle international institutions of justice must be fiercely resisted and rejected.

Nancy Okail is president and CEO of the Center for International Policy.

articles.title: Ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump takes effect in Russian-occupied southern Ukraine town
articles.summary: A localized ceasefire agreement between Ukraine and Russia took effect on Tuesday after first lady Melania Trump announced last week she secured a temporary humanitarian agreement for the border city of Oleshky. The Russian-occupied town is located in southern Ukraine, and residents have faced shortages in food and medicine amid the ongoing war. The pause…
articles.body:
A localized ceasefire agreement between Ukraine and Russia took effect on Tuesday after first lady Melania Trump announced last week she secured a temporary humanitarian agreement for the border city of Oleshky.

The Russian-occupied town is located in southern Ukraine, and residents have faced shortages in food and medicine amid the ongoing war .

The pause in hostilities began at 3 a.m. local time and is set to last through Saturday to allow for a humanitarian mission to be carried out, according to authorities on both sides of the conflict.

Around 2,000 people are reportedly trapped in the city, including a large elderly population, because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the region.

The first lady characterized Oleshky as a “front-line war city on the brink of disaster” in a press release announcing the ceasefire agreement Friday.

“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks,” Trump said in a statement. “It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”

She brokered the agreement between Russia and Ukraine with the support of Pope Leo XIV. The humanitarian mission includes sending in doctors, food and other aid to the city before an evacuation corridor is opened.

Outside of Oleshky, the war has waged on, with Russian forces hitting a university campus in Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 12 others, according to local officials.

Authorities in Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city, said Russian attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the country’s energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure were under attack in 11 different regions.

“Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation,” he wrote on social media . “Pressure on Russia and real support for Ukraine are needed to change the situation.”

“I thank everyone who truly supports our efforts to protect lives and understands the importance of support packages arriving on time,” Zelensky continued. “We must bring peace closer and save lives.”

Russian authorities said a drone attack near the country’s border with Ukraine killed one person and injured 30 others.

Both sides deny deliberately targeting citizens in the ongoing conflict, which has lasted for more than four years.

The aid mission in Oleshky comes ahead of planned trilateral talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia to bring this war to a close. The negotiations are scheduled for next month in Abu Dhabi.

articles.title: Lebanon’s lost olive season: harvesting olives under drones and warplanes
articles.summary: Lebanon’s olive harvesters are facing dangerous conditions, with potential attacks and fear of cluster munitions.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – Every year, Khaled Farhat tends to his olive trees in the southern village of Majdel Selm, a task carried out year after year amid the din of war.

“I own an olive grove with about 200 trees. I tend to them in my spare time whenever I’m not on duty at the school,” he told Al Jazeera by phone.

This year, reaching his olive grove, which is just a 20-minute drive from the border with Israel, is more complicated due to the ongoing Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon. His town of Majdel Selm lies just north of Israel’s “Yellow Line ”, below which the Israeli military is demolishing homes and local infrastructure.

To reach his land, Farhat said, he had to request access from his local municipality, which forwarded the request to the Lebanese Army. The army then coordinates with a mechanism established after June’s Tripartite Framework Agreement between the United States, Israel and Lebanon to get permits for locals to tend to their olive groves.

American University of Beirut’s Ramy Zurayk, a professor specialising in landscape design and ecosystem management, said the widespread damage to farms and buildings in southern Lebanon, along with restrictions on movement, is an attempt by Israel to make the area “sterile”.

“The Israeli project is to eliminate humans and living organisms from the land,” Zurayk told Al Jazeera. “They are doing this via a variety of methods, including destroying the habitat and the components of the landscape that provide life, which destroy the relationship between the people and this land.”

Many of the border areas’ olive trees have been burned to the ground or uprooted by Israeli bulldozers. Lebanon’s Environment Minister Tamara Elzein said more than 16,000 hectares (about 40,000 acres) of land have been torched since Israel began bombing, and later invading, Lebanon in October 2023, including through the use of white phosphorus , a highly flammable substance.

Israel continues to occupy nearly 630sq km (243sq miles) of southern Lebanon, which includes swaths of farmland and dozens of villages.

In areas where the olive groves are still intact, Israel’s occupation has complicated this season’s harvest. Farmers and landowners say they work with Israeli drones flying overhead and live with the fear of unexploded ordnance on the ground. An hour earlier, an Israeli shell had landed near Farhat.

“Drones are constantly in the sky. You look up and see one, two, three of them sometimes just moving back and forth,” Farhat said. “Warplanes sometimes pass by and carry out strikes nearby, taking a toll on us psychologically and emotionally.”

Israel has placed tight restrictions on Lebanese farmers’ access to their land, which has cost them their crops. Farhat said he was given just a two-week window to work his land, and the neglect of his farmland is already evident.

“Usually, there shouldn’t be any weeds. But since the time for tilling and clearing the land happened during our displacement, we weren’t able to clear it. The land remained as it was because we couldn’t reach it,” he said.

“We’re in the middle of the harvest now. If we manage to finish harvesting everything directly from the trees within this timeframe, then great. Otherwise, whatever remains will go unharvested.”

The time spent clearing these weeds eats into the limited time he has to pick his olives. But they could also conceal a deadly surprise. Farmers and landowners said working their lands in the south is rife with unexploded ordnance, including from cluster bombs.

In early October, at least two people were killed in olive groves in south Lebanon. A retired soldier was killed in Yater village in the Bint Jbeil district by Israeli artillery fire. Another young man, who worked as an engineer, was killed when Israeli ordnance exploded while he was harvesting olives in the village of Froun , also in Bint Jbeil. A day later, a member of Lebanon’s police force tending to farmland in the southern village of Ain Ebel, a predominantly Christian village, was also killed in an explosion.

“There is a constant fear of being targeted [by Israeli attacks], especially in areas near the sites of attacks, as well as the risk of encountering cluster bombs or other remnants of war, which pose a grave danger to human life,” Hicham Hoteit, a journalist and olive farmer from Babliyeh town in south Lebanon, told Al Jazeera.

Explosives have been a recurring problem for farmers in southern Lebanon since the final days of the 2006 war, when Israeli forces dumped cluster bombs containing between 2.6 and four million submunitions in the area, according to a Human Rights Watch report.

“One of the biggest challenges we’ve seen in southern Lebanon since the 2006 war is how long cluster munitions continue to affect people’s lives long after conflict has taken place,” Hiba Ghandour, Lebanon’s programme manager for the Mines Advisory Group (MAG), a nongovernmental organisation that aids communities affected by landmines, unexploded ordnance, small arms and light weapons, told Al Jazeera.

“Millions of submunitions were scattered across the region, including farmland, and many failed to explode on impact. They were left hidden in fields, olive groves and orchards – many of which we are still clearing today.”

According to a 2022 Lebanese Mine Action Center (LMAC) report, the government announced that much of the contaminated land had been cleared. “The Lebanese government announced that only 5 million square metres of land remained contaminated with cluster munitions [18 percent of the baseline to be cleared],” Ghandour said, citing the report.

“Since October 2023, the situation has become more complex. The latest hostilities have added a new layer of explosive hazards.”

Ghandour said MAG had identified 444,000sq metres of confirmed hazardous areas for farmers, but with research still ongoing, this figure is likely to rise significantly.

Despite these dangers, Lebanon’s dire economic situation has pushed many Lebanese to work their lands out of necessity.

“In our experience, clearing agricultural land is especially challenging, as the contamination can be concealed within vegetation or beneath soil, which takes us longer to clear,” Ghandour said.

“When people are under pressure to earn a living, they often feel they have no choice but to return to their land before it has been made safe, making clearance all the more challenging. Repeated bombardment has also damaged agricultural land and made it harder for our clearance teams to reach some of the communities most in need.”

Political analyst Bassel Doueik told Al Jazeera that many Lebanese citizens have been harassed by Israeli forces and barred from harvesting their olive trees.

Doueik used Kfarshouba, a predominantly Sunni border village, as an example. On Monday, he said, about 200 Israeli soldiers entered Kfarshouba and searched houses in several neighbourhoods, while at least three Merkava tanks and other military vehicles infiltrated the area around the village.

The widespread use of white phosphorus has led some Lebanese to hesitate buying produce from the south over concerns that it could be exposed to hazardous chemicals.

Zurayk, the AUB academic, said in a panel hosted at his university on October 21 that the panic was unfounded and there was no evidence that any of the olives or other produce from south Lebanon was dangerous to consume.

For many in Lebanon, including in areas beyond the south, harvesting olives is serious work but is also an opportunity for their families or communities to come together.

Many people with farmland across south Lebanon have said this year, due to the threat of Israeli attacks, they will leave their children and other relatives behind when they head to their crops. Back in Majdel Selm, Farhat said the dangers are evident in the south this harvest season.

“People hear that the situation is dangerous, they hear that there is shelling, but for someone who is actually in the midst of the shelling, or living under it, it is certainly a different experience,” he said.

“The reality on the ground is something else entirely. Still, thank God, hopefully, this is just a phase that will pass. Hopefully, the situation will not escalate further and will begin to de-escalate and move towards something better.”

articles.title: US assigns nuclear submarine to Australia under AUKUS as China expands Pacific footprint
articles.summary: The Pentagon has designated the USS Colorado as the first US Navy submarine to join an Australian-based rotational force, strengthening Washington's
articles.body: The Pentagon has designated the USS Colorado as the first US Navy submarine to join an Australian-based rotational force, strengthening Washington's undersea military posture in the Indo-Pacific as the US and its allies seek to deter China's growing naval influence in the region.US defence secretary Pete Hegseth announced the selection alongside Australian deputy Prime Minister and defence minister Richard Marles and British defence secretary John Healey, according to a joint statement issued by the three countries.The Virginia-class USS Colorado fast-attack submarine is scheduled to join Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-West) in late 2027 at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia.The rotational force is expected to host up to four US fast-attack submarines and one British submarine, expanding maintenance and support facilities for allied undersea operations in the Indo-Pacific.The arrangement is part of AUKUS, the trilateral security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States established in 2021.AUKUS aims to help Australia develop its own fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarines while deepening defence cooperation among the three allies. The move also carries wider strategic significance as Washington seeks to strengthen regional deterrence and complicate China's military planning across the Pacific.About USS ColoradoThe USS Colorado (SSN 788) is a Virginia-class Block III nuclear-powered fast-attack submarine of the US Navy, commissioned in 2018.Measuring 377 feet and a submerged displacement of approximately 7,800 tons, the submarine can travel at speeds exceeding 25 knots (around 46 km/h) underwater. It is powered by a nuclear reactor and designed for extended operations without frequent refuelling.The submarine's weapons include two large-diameter Virginia Payload Tubes, each capable of launching six Tomahawk cruise missiles, giving it a capacity of up to 12 missiles through these tubes.It is also equipped with four torpedo tubes that can fire Mk 48 Advanced Capability torpedoes against enemy submarines and surface vessels. These capabilities allow the USS Colorado to conduct precision strikes, anti-submarine warfare and other undersea combat missions.Beyond its weapons, the USS Colorado is designed for intelligence gathering, surveillance, reconnaissance and support for special operations forces. Its combination of stealth, endurance and strike capability makes it a valuable asset for sustained undersea operations.China expands its Pacific footprintChina has steadily expanded its diplomatic, economic and security presence across the Pacific, challenging the traditional strategic influence of Australia and the United States in a region critical to their defence planning.A June 2026 report by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), Pressure Points Part 3, said Beijing was building a wider pattern of military access, security cooperation and regional influence across the Southwest Pacific and Australia's maritime approaches. The report noted that China's expanding blue-water navy, policing partnerships and overseas access arrangements were reshaping regional security dynamics.One of the biggest concerns for Canberra and Washington is China's 2022 security agreement with the Solomon Islands. articles.body:
Political commentator Bill O’Reilly on Monday predicted that the U.S. could have its own protests similar to those that have broken out in recent weeks across France and other parts of Europe, but “on steroids.”

“On Balance” host Leland Vittert asked O’Reilly on NewsNation, The Hill’s broadcast partner, about seeming to be worried about greater ramifications if President Trump cannot address issues like the cost of living.

“I’m not worried about the individuals, I’m worried about the country because if the voters in the country are this dumb, that they don’t know what’s coming around a pike –– oh my God, we’re in for France on steroids, we’re gonna be France if this continues,” the former Fox News host said.

O’Reilly added that he does not expect the president to change course, saying “that’s not what he does.”

“I believe most Americans have made up their minds,” he continued. “There is going to be the crew that hates Trump and the crew that likes Trump. And –– isn’t this interesting –– this midterm is going to be about Trump. That’s what it’s going to be about.”

France has seen waves of protests and rioting after more than 400,000 people took to the streets. University students marched to challenge what they say are worsening school conditions and the cost of living, with that frustration boiling over into clashes with police.

Marches saw some peaceful demonstrations, but French law enforcement have arrested about 2,400 people in connection with some of the violence and looting.

French Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste on Monday pledged to make “substantial change,” with ministers pledging 4 billion euros ($4.5 billion) in loans for school renovations, smaller classes, more job opportunities for teachers and for more student grants. But the deadline for these changes, in 2028, lands just after French President Emmanuel Macron leaves office.

The National Rally party, the political faction belonging to far-right leader Marine Le Pen, has sought to make the unrest stirred by these conditions a part of her presidential campaign. Polling shows Le Pen leading ahead of the country’s first round of voting in April.

American officials like Trump and Vice President Vance have blamed the protests on mass migration from the Middle East and Africa to Europe. Trump has attempted to tie these protests to what he claims could happen in the U.S. if Democrats win majorities in Congress after the midterm elections.

Macron told reporters last week that such suggestions made by leaders in the U.S. or right-wing leaders in Europe were “ unacceptable and even stupid .”

“For me, there is no visible foreign interference in the events that took place,” Macron said in Doha, Qatar, according to Al Jazeera. “On the other hand, there was foreign manipulation of information which led to unacceptable and even stupid comments by many, including foreign leaders.”
